#### He explicitly says an institutional tag does not guarantee pay

He identifies rent, staff, utilities and connectivity as costs and estimates roughly INR 60000-100000 monthly in his Noida context, recommending around six months' runway and a several-lakh reserve.

#### Advertised compensation may differ from the final offer

The speakers debate present pay and negotiation, and he urges earlier independent practice once clinically competent rather than staying in corporate work indefinitely.

Context: He admits not knowing current SR pay; vague corporate ranges and his career preference are not universal market evidence.

#### Long-term practice growth is variable rather than automatic compounding

She describes the possibility of a recognised clinician eventually developing a large practice or hospital, and says the branch title does not itself generate income.

Dr. Meenakshi Bothra, paediatrician and medical educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [55:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Zuy8C9je0Xc&t=3337s)

#### Home safety, online information and delayed presentations

He recounts an accidental medication ingestion, discusses limited caregiver time and worries about misinformation or treatment by unqualified people before specialist assessment. His message is timely, competent care with correct paediatric dosing.

Dr Pankaj Tikku; host anecdotes and supplied statistics distinguished separately · [40:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P3PrJhWjYCs&t=2444s)

#### He preferred a stable clinic base over many scattered OPDs

A friend advised planning a six-month reserve, starting a clinic when competent and remaining in one location rather than rotating among hospitals. He reports breaking even around six months.

#### Paediatric opportunities depend on location and service model

She sees increasing competition as training numbers expand. She thinks general paediatrics can still support a career outside major metros, while specialist training may provide an edge in a metro corporate market.

Using paediatric versus adult nephrology, she notes that disease patterns and referral awareness can reduce the number of potential patients in some child-focused niches.

#### Overseas possibilities are raised without a complete pathway

He personally favours paediatric cardiology's prospects and describes possible UK/US and UAE opportunities, while admitting uncertainty about UAE recognition. He also sees growing opportunities within India.

#### Informal institution suggestions require exact-name checks

#### She did not personally witness the most severe political harm described

She acknowledges that favouritism and interpersonal tensions can exist, but says she did not see the severe pressure-driven departures posed by the host. She cautions against attributing a departure to one cause without knowing the circumstances.

### Shared training and wider residency discussion

These are general preparation or training discussions, not findings about the specialty as a whole.

#### Proposed reforms include caregiver support, vaccine safety and stress practice

He proposes earlier preparation for difficult clinical situations, maternal/child-health learning, properly equipped vaccination centres, correct cold-chain/administration practices and supported practice in responding to stress, drawing an analogy with pilot simulation.

Dr Pankaj Tikku; host anecdotes and supplied statistics distinguished separately · [49:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P3PrJhWjYCs&t=2980s)

Context: Suggested certificate durations and proposed graduation requirements are his ideas, not current mandatory rules.

#### Separate genuine interest from assumptions about job security

He describes liking science, biology and learning about the body, personal experience of asthma, and a childhood wish to become a doctor. Perceptions of engineering unemployment and medicine's stability reinforced the decision.

Context: Disliking mathematics is not sufficient reason to choose medicine, and no degree guarantees employment or an easy financial path.

#### A practical target can change without defining your worth

He initially hoped for AIIMS but adjusted his entrance target after seeing competition, then later entered AIIMS and found more extracurricular activity than he had expected.

Context: Entrance ranks and cohort comparisons are personal history, not proof of intelligence, human worth or superiority of one institution.

#### A high-rank story is not a universal preparation formula

He recalls becoming much more focused in the final school year after personal and family changes and setting a goal of qualifying without a repeat year.

Dr. Aditya Sanjay Gupta describes AIIMS education, paediatrics training and interest in paediatric haematology/oncology; host comments and jokes remain separate. Captions are often corrupted and lack reliable speaker labels. · [7:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yspL0IQ-NzE&t=467s)

Context: His statement that he wasted no moments is retrospective rhetoric, not a reason to eliminate rest or assume a repeat year is failure.

#### He explicitly rejects ragging despite positive personal memories

He first recalls fear and later describes some initiation experiences as friendly, but repeatedly says ragging should not be done because boundaries can be crossed and harmful outcomes occur.

Context: Positive recollection does not justify forced undressing, sexualised jokes, intimidation or abuse; friendship can be built without ragging.

#### Respect does not create an obligation to obey personal demands

The host discusses hierarchy and says harassment and hitting juniors are wrong, while also expressing a view that senior requests should be obeyed.

Dr. Aditya Sanjay Gupta describes AIIMS education, paediatrics training and interest in paediatric haematology/oncology; host comments and jokes remain separate. Captions are often corrupted and lack reliable speaker labels. · [11:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yspL0IQ-NzE&t=690s)

Context: The host's obedience framing is not endorsed. Neither seniority nor a claim of friendly interaction authorises coercion, violence or financial demands.

#### An entrance result does not replace regular learning

After relaxing initially, he found the first medical examination difficult and began studying more consistently because he wanted to understand medicine rather than scrape through after cramming.

He found the diagnostic knowledge portrayed in House inspiring and wanted command of the subject, explicitly distinguishing that from the character's professional manner.

- [Overseas possibilities are raised without a complete pathway · 23:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=P3PrJhWjYCs&t=1394s) — Dr Pankaj Tikku; host anecdotes and supplied statistics distinguished separately · Full caption summary

## General Medicine

5/5 mapped primary episodes have full-caption summaries; 0 have partial selected-caption briefs; 0 related episodes mapped separately.

Personal fit (editorial): Do I enjoy broad diagnostic responsibility, acute illness and potentially further training?

### Fit & daily work

Which parts of the actual work would I enjoy?

#### His pathway included overseas MBBS, teaching and several training changes

He describes overseas undergraduate study after unsuccessful Indian entry attempts, briefly taking pathology, teaching and writing a book before completing MD Medicine. He then left a short oncology super-specialty period after deciding he wanted his own work rather than another credential.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [2:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=139s)

Context: Autobiographical chronology and institution/qualification names are not independently checked; leaving training does not confer the abandoned specialist qualification.

Question to investigate (editorial): What work are you seeking from a qualification, and what are the costs of switching or leaving a seat?

#### Clinical breadth and mechanisms were the attraction

He recalls reading a second-hand Harrison during undergraduate years and wanting medicine even when other branches were available. He says completing the desired branch gave him personal satisfaction.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [6:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=391s)

Context: His path is not proof that only a dream branch can lead to a satisfying career.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do you enjoy integrating mechanisms, diagnosis and treatment across systems?

#### He strongly prioritises branch over institution

Using a marriage-venue analogy, he argues that a specialty remains with the doctor longer than the institution's name and advises choosing the preferred branch even at a less prestigious college.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [7:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=451s)

Context: His claim that college makes little difference and compromise means lifelong unhappiness is overbroad; training quality and changing preferences matter.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does the preferred branch also meet minimum standards for supervision, case mix, safety and affordability?

#### Another doctor's switch encouraged him to try again

He was encouraged by an older senior who left CTVS for radiology and appeared happier with the new work pattern. He accepted that medicine might offer less favourable work-life balance but suited his own interests.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [9:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=593s)

Context: The radiology lifestyle comparison is anecdotal; interest does not eliminate fatigue, health needs or family costs.

Question to investigate (editorial): What actual schedules and responsibilities would you accept for work you value?

#### New cases and integrated reading keep medicine interesting for him

He likes gaining some understanding across specialties and following basic science through to treatment. He describes repeated reading becoming rewarding and new cases prompting study after work rather than a monotonous routine.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=656s)

Context: Enthusiasm does not replace protected learning time, supervision or access to current clinical guidance.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do variety, diagnostic uncertainty and continuous study energise you?

#### He values enjoyment of teaching over a quick earnings motive

He suggests new educators focus on engaging classes and feedback rather than demanding high initial pay, even mentioning free early teaching. He expects reputation to develop if learners respond well.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [33:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2000s)

Context: Passion does not guarantee income or justify indefinite unpaid work; clear terms and sustainable workload matter.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would you enjoy preparation and teaching even before a large audience or high fee exists?

#### He sees money as important for autonomy but not worth losing health

He values financial security, a home, peace of mind and enough resources to choose how to use time. He rejects both pretending money does not matter and sacrificing mental or physical health for unlimited accumulation.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [13:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=823s)

Context: His priorities are personal, and no universal income amount follows from this reflection. Housing and security needs vary.

Question to investigate (editorial): What level of financial security would support the life I want without consuming it?

#### Competing expectations and emotional depletion can create isolation

He describes being judged for earning, charging, buying things or not earning enough, then using much of his emotional energy with seriously ill patients and families. At home he may struggle to listen well, and nonmedical friends may assume a doctor cannot be distressed.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [17:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=1043s)

Context: These are personal and broad impressions, not comparative loneliness prevalence. A career setback does not mean lifelong depression, and seeking mental-health care should not be stigmatized.

Question to investigate (editorial): What peer, family and professional support would help me recover and communicate after difficult work?

#### He links niche, geography and independence to the pace of practice growth

He argues that building a general practice in a smaller town differs from pursuing a highly specialized transplant career in South Delhi. He says he trained until able to do his core work independently and then avoided prolonged subordinate practice. He uses monthly earnings aspirations, including INR 5 lakh, to challenge what he sees as underpayment.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [23:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=1427s)

Context: No small-town hospital timeline or monthly figure is a guarantee. His pay expectations are not a salary survey, and complex team-based work may legitimately require extended supported development.

Question to investigate (editorial): What local demand, capital, referral structure and supervision does my intended scope require?

#### Word of mouth is a meaningful feedback signal for him

He says he still works long days because seeing patients is satisfying, especially when a new patient comes on the recommendation of someone who improved. He treats this as a sign his work made a difference.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [43:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=2608s)

Context: Patient referrals and satisfaction do not by themselves establish treatment efficacy. Personal enjoyment does not make fourteen-hour days safe or necessary for others.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which parts of clinical work would remain rewarding after the novelty fades?

#### Teaching experience and a consistent content schedule support his online work

He describes an aim of one YouTube video and several reels weekly and says adapting to social media is part of his growth plan. Experience teaching helps him explain ideas in ordinary language. Testing a different kind of work also challenged inherited limits on what he thought he could do.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [44:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=2662s)

Context: His claim that social media is essential for everyone is not established. A sound practice does not require influencer-scale visibility.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would public education fit my skills and workload, and what accurate, sustainable output can I maintain?

#### A diagnostic recovery made medicine meaningful

He describes sibling comparison, an accident that sharpened his focus and an internship case in which diagnosing severe hypothyroidism helped an older homeless woman recover. Diagnostic reasoning and tangible patient benefit became stronger motivations than the initial family comparison.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [5:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=355s)

Context: The retrospective case contains ASR errors and is not treatment guidance.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which real clinical experiences make this field meaningful to me?

#### Personal limitations, family input and multiple future pathways

He considered dermatology, radiology, surgery and pediatrics. Tremor and anxiety around blood discouraged surgery; family input and the breadth of later pathways favored medicine, which he calls a launchpad.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [7:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=466s)

Context: His symptoms and family advice are individual circumstances; current superspecialty eligibility needs official verification.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would I still enjoy general medicine if I never obtain the particular DM seat I imagine?

#### Enjoying complexity and uncertainty matters

His suggested mindset includes lifelong learning, interest in unresolved diagnostic problems, stamina for a hectic first year and openness to DM. He contrasts this with choosing a branch for glamour.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [10:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=629s)

Context: His DM preference is not a universal requirement. Health or fatigue needs should not be treated as moral failings.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do I enjoy uncertain diagnoses and repeated reassessment as much as a correct answer?

#### Recovery and diagnostic curiosity are personal sources of fulfillment

He recalls an ICU patient recovering and returning with a wedding invitation, and a brain-abscess case where he proposed a possible infection source. These stories convey emotional reward and investigative satisfaction.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [55:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=3302s)

Context: The makeup-brush infection source was a theory rather than proven causation. These are not clinical instructions.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do continuity, uncertainty and gradual recovery motivate me as much as dramatic rescue stories?

#### Emotional restraint, a mental-health break and a return to residency

He rejects the idea that doctors become heartless, saying restrained behavior can coexist with guilt and distress. He recalls a seven-day break when he considered quitting and family encouraged him to return, then celebrates his marriage and urges sincere work.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [57:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=3425s)

Context: Showing emotion is not proof of guilt or weakness. His return after apologizing is one story, not a rule to remain in harmful conditions.

Question to investigate (editorial): How will I recognize distress early and seek help without equating endurance with success?

#### Medicine attracted her through family example, patient connection and learning

She describes two doctor parents, admiration for her father's clinical life, enjoyment of biology and reading, and comfort building relationships with people.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=193s)

Context: Childhood fascination and a doctor family are individual influences, not requirements for competence or proof that long absences from home are desirable.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which everyday tasks attract me beyond admiration for a role model?

#### She would reconsider psychiatry despite genuine enjoyment of medicine

She recalls psychiatry as an early interest but felt that a high rank should be spent on a prestigious branch. Family and social stigma made choosing it harder; one supportive person might have changed her decision.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [5:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=344s)

Context: Her regret is a personal comparison, not evidence that psychiatry is universally better or that she dislikes all internal medicine. Child psychiatry and psychology have distinct training and professional scopes.

Question to investigate (editorial): Am I rejecting a fitting specialty because of prestige, rank expectations or stigma?

#### The loss of broad internal medicine is her central dissatisfaction

She loves the breadth of internal medicine and reading across its subjects. In a narrowed superspecialty role, other teams and patient expectations can limit how broadly she practices, reducing her own satisfaction.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [8:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=498s)

Context: This describes her work model, not a universal prohibition on a specialist managing other problems. Competence, privileges, referral need and current rules determine actual scope.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do I prefer broad diagnostic responsibility or a focused specialist role?

#### Family and peer expectations helped push her toward superspecialization

She says family pressure, peers doing DM and fear that entry would become harder made stopping after MD feel unacceptable. The host identifies this as a common audience concern.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [10:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=605s)

Context: The host's 80-percent framing is not supported by a representative survey. Further training can be valuable but is not automatically compulsory for every MD/DNB physician.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would I choose further training if the prestige and peer pressure disappeared?

#### Her ordered specialty preferences are explicitly subjective

Asked for a best-to-worst order she puts rheumatology/immunology first and nephrology next, acknowledges her bias, then discusses cardiology, gastro/hepatology, endocrinology and pulmonology.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [37:27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=2247s)

Context: This is not a validated all-parameter ranking or pay comparison. Precision medicine, biologics and gene therapy are not interchangeable, and her future claims are uncertain.

Question to investigate (editorial): What actual tasks, training and evidence support my own shortlist?

#### Internal medicine can involve repeated grief and abrupt emotional transitions

She says attachment develops through repeated rounds and contact with patients and families. Breaking news of a death can bring the doctor close to tears. She describes moving between terminal illness, family worries and obstetric critical-care situations within the same working day.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [27:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=1650s)

Context: These are personal experiences, not evidence that all clinicians react the same way or that visible emotion proves ethical care. Support and boundaries matter alongside empathy.

Question to investigate (editorial): How do I respond to emotional uncertainty, and what supervision, peer support and recovery would I need?

#### He advises completing relevant PG training before becoming an educator

He began teaching during internship but now thinks specialty training provides deeper roots and clinical examples beyond repeating short notes. He describes discomfort at being a teacher without MD and argues for subject expertise.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [31:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=1898s)

Context: MBBS is not nothing, and a degree alone does not guarantee teaching quality; actual eligibility depends on the role.

Question to investigate (editorial): What subject knowledge, teaching skill and appropriate credentials would support your intended role?

#### A busy clinician inspired his emphasis on courtesy and reputation

He recounts a senior ENT clinician with a busy clinic, newer therapy and a fee waiver for a doctor's relative. He saw the gesture as building trust and word-of-mouth.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [34:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2093s)

Context: Anecdotal daily receipts of INR 1-1.5 lakh are not personal profit or typical earnings. Newer medication and courtesy do not prove superior treatment.

Question to investigate (editorial): How can respectful evidence-based care and fair fee policies build trust without commercial pressure?

#### Listening and affordability are central to his practice model

He emphasizes greeting patients, detailed history, listening and tailoring investigations to need and affordability. He sees useful public content as a way to become familiar, but says excessive investigations undermine outpatient practice.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [47:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2845s)

Context: Informal medication comments are not prescribing advice. Patient preference does not replace evidence-based care; visibility is not competence.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I explain uncertainty and medication use, and build trust without overtesting or overselling?

#### Teaching can mean long travel days and uncertain demand

He describes 9-to-9 classes, packed bags and travel that initially feels attractive but can be tiring. He worries about changing examination markets and younger teachers competing, which encouraged an independent clinical practice.

#### He favours local footfall and a manageable journey from home

He recommends studying demand where doctors already cluster, not assuming a place without doctors is automatically attractive. He wants the clinic near enough for access but separate enough to protect home boundaries, noting heavy Delhi traffic.

#### Teaching interest, corporate insecurity and building a backup

Question to investigate (editorial): Do I want public teaching, salaried clinical work or the business responsibilities of practice?

#### A successful teaching partnership still ended after relocation

He recalls a coaching venture operating from 2017 to 2022 with a partner whose mindset and patience matched his. It closed after the partner moved abroad, illustrating dependence on personal circumstances as well as compatibility.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [47:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2859s)

Context: Unverified commercial success claims do not establish a typical partnership return.

Question to investigate (editorial): Have partners agreed roles, investment, cover, conflict resolution and an exit plan?

#### He lowered his consultation fee to make repeat care more affordable

He recounts fees ranging from INR 300 to INR 1,000 across earlier locations and INR 500 at the newer clinic. He says a lower price felt more acceptable to returning patients and resisted copying a neighbouring surgeon's fee.

Question to investigate (editorial): What fair, transparent fee can sustain adequate consultation time and access?

#### He did not experience medicine saturation; preferred location still matters

He reports no personal difficulty finding medicine work but acknowledges competition for premium metropolitan posts. He suggests smaller-city general practice may offer demand and income, while family resources, lifestyle preferences and superspecialty referral patterns can favor a metro.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [38:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2324s)

Question to investigate (editorial): Which locations can I commit to, and what do recent graduates and actual vacancies there show?

#### She favours starting a clinic early while respecting competence and contracts

She calls private practice a long-term process that may begin with very few patients and suggests part-time evening OPD alongside paid work when the contract allows it. She favours beginning early rather than expecting immediate attendance.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [37:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=2270s)

Context: Earlier is not always safer or better. Clinical competence, registration, facility requirements, fatigue, household needs and employer rules still apply, and growth is not guaranteed.

Question to investigate (editorial): Am I clinically ready, contractually permitted and financially prepared for a gradual start?

### Benefits described

What did these speakers value, and under which conditions?

#### Clinical breadth and mechanisms were the attraction

He recalls reading a second-hand Harrison during undergraduate years and wanting medicine even when other branches were available. He says completing the desired branch gave him personal satisfaction.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [6:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=391s)

Context: His path is not proof that only a dream branch can lead to a satisfying career.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do you enjoy integrating mechanisms, diagnosis and treatment across systems?

#### New cases and integrated reading keep medicine interesting for him

He likes gaining some understanding across specialties and following basic science through to treatment. He describes repeated reading becoming rewarding and new cases prompting study after work rather than a monotonous routine.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [10:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=656s)

Context: Enthusiasm does not replace protected learning time, supervision or access to current clinical guidance.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do variety, diagnostic uncertainty and continuous study energise you?

#### Word of mouth is a meaningful feedback signal for him

He says he still works long days because seeing patients is satisfying, especially when a new patient comes on the recommendation of someone who improved. He treats this as a sign his work made a difference.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [43:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=2608s)

Context: Patient referrals and satisfaction do not by themselves establish treatment efficacy. Personal enjoyment does not make fourteen-hour days safe or necessary for others.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which parts of clinical work would remain rewarding after the novelty fades?

#### A diagnostic recovery made medicine meaningful

He describes sibling comparison, an accident that sharpened his focus and an internship case in which diagnosing severe hypothyroidism helped an older homeless woman recover. Diagnostic reasoning and tangible patient benefit became stronger motivations than the initial family comparison.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [5:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=355s)

Context: The retrospective case contains ASR errors and is not treatment guidance.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which real clinical experiences make this field meaningful to me?

#### Recovery and diagnostic curiosity are personal sources of fulfillment

He recalls an ICU patient recovering and returning with a wedding invitation, and a brain-abscess case where he proposed a possible infection source. These stories convey emotional reward and investigative satisfaction.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [55:02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=3302s)

Context: The makeup-brush infection source was a theory rather than proven causation. These are not clinical instructions.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do continuity, uncertainty and gradual recovery motivate me as much as dramatic rescue stories?

#### Medicine attracted her through family example, patient connection and learning

She describes two doctor parents, admiration for her father's clinical life, enjoyment of biology and reading, and comfort building relationships with people.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [3:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=193s)

Context: Childhood fascination and a doctor family are individual influences, not requirements for competence or proof that long absences from home are desirable.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which everyday tasks attract me beyond admiration for a role model?

#### He sees supportive teams as a way beyond one doctor's limited hours

He praises examples from AIG of senior doctors identifying and promoting juniors' strengths. He contrasts this with fear that another clinician will take away a practice, which can leave the owner working late into older age.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [39:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=2377s)

Context: His claims about largest or only institutions are not verified rankings, and broad claims that doctors are bad at teamwork are opinion rather than evidence.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does the institution share cases, develop juniors and provide trustworthy cover?

#### She sees a continuing role for coordinated generalist care

She challenges using GP as a disparaging label and describes older patients frustrated by fragmented multispecialty visits. She expects broad coordinated care to become more valuable.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [11:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=705s)

Context: An MD physician and an MBBS general practitioner are not identical qualifications. Her two-decade forecast and legal restrictions are not verified policy, and some referrals are necessary for safe care rather than needless fragmentation.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would I enjoy integrating multiple problems and coordinating specialist input?

### Trade-offs & challenges

Which demands and compromises could I accept?

#### His pathway included overseas MBBS, teaching and several training changes

He describes overseas undergraduate study after unsuccessful Indian entry attempts, briefly taking pathology, teaching and writing a book before completing MD Medicine. He then left a short oncology super-specialty period after deciding he wanted his own work rather than another credential.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [2:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=139s)

Context: Autobiographical chronology and institution/qualification names are not independently checked; leaving training does not confer the abandoned specialist qualification.

Question to investigate (editorial): What work are you seeking from a qualification, and what are the costs of switching or leaving a seat?

#### He strongly prioritises branch over institution

Using a marriage-venue analogy, he argues that a specialty remains with the doctor longer than the institution's name and advises choosing the preferred branch even at a less prestigious college.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [7:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=451s)

Context: His claim that college makes little difference and compromise means lifelong unhappiness is overbroad; training quality and changing preferences matter.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does the preferred branch also meet minimum standards for supervision, case mix, safety and affordability?

#### Another doctor's switch encouraged him to try again

He was encouraged by an older senior who left CTVS for radiology and appeared happier with the new work pattern. He accepted that medicine might offer less favourable work-life balance but suited his own interests.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [9:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=593s)

Context: The radiology lifestyle comparison is anecdotal; interest does not eliminate fatigue, health needs or family costs.

Question to investigate (editorial): What actual schedules and responsibilities would you accept for work you value?

#### He values enjoyment of teaching over a quick earnings motive

He suggests new educators focus on engaging classes and feedback rather than demanding high initial pay, even mentioning free early teaching. He expects reputation to develop if learners respond well.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [33:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2000s)

Context: Passion does not guarantee income or justify indefinite unpaid work; clear terms and sustainable workload matter.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would you enjoy preparation and teaching even before a large audience or high fee exists?

#### He sees money as important for autonomy but not worth losing health

He values financial security, a home, peace of mind and enough resources to choose how to use time. He rejects both pretending money does not matter and sacrificing mental or physical health for unlimited accumulation.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [13:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=823s)

Context: His priorities are personal, and no universal income amount follows from this reflection. Housing and security needs vary.

Question to investigate (editorial): What level of financial security would support the life I want without consuming it?

#### The host challenges the long training-to-income delay

The host asks whether medicine's long effort and delayed rewards deter students. Vatsya emphasizes hard work and says independent practice can become financially strong after years, giving annual examples around INR 1-1.5 crore for some established practitioners. The host points out the long training period before those years begin.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [14:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=889s)

Context: These are optimistic personal estimates, not a representative income survey. They concern independent practice, not resident stipend or employee salary, and do not show gross versus net consistently.

Question to investigate (editorial): What are my realistic training costs, earnings delay and alternative opportunities?

#### Competing expectations and emotional depletion can create isolation

He describes being judged for earning, charging, buying things or not earning enough, then using much of his emotional energy with seriously ill patients and families. At home he may struggle to listen well, and nonmedical friends may assume a doctor cannot be distressed.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [17:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=1043s)

Context: These are personal and broad impressions, not comparative loneliness prevalence. A career setback does not mean lifelong depression, and seeking mental-health care should not be stigmatized.

Question to investigate (editorial): What peer, family and professional support would help me recover and communicate after difficult work?

#### Emotional restraint, a mental-health break and a return to residency

He rejects the idea that doctors become heartless, saying restrained behavior can coexist with guilt and distress. He recalls a seven-day break when he considered quitting and family encouraged him to return, then celebrates his marriage and urges sincere work.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [57:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=3425s)

Context: Showing emotion is not proof of guilt or weakness. His return after apologizing is one story, not a rule to remain in harmful conditions.

Question to investigate (editorial): How will I recognize distress early and seek help without equating endurance with success?

#### She would reconsider psychiatry despite genuine enjoyment of medicine

She recalls psychiatry as an early interest but felt that a high rank should be spent on a prestigious branch. Family and social stigma made choosing it harder; one supportive person might have changed her decision.

#### The loss of broad internal medicine is her central dissatisfaction

She loves the breadth of internal medicine and reading across its subjects. In a narrowed superspecialty role, other teams and patient expectations can limit how broadly she practices, reducing her own satisfaction.

#### He supports fair consultation fees while describing his own affordability concerns

He thinks established doctors in Delhi or Mumbai may charge around INR 1500-2000 and should not automatically equate higher fees with greed. Yet he says he held his own consultation fee for eight years partly to retain access for lower-income patients and is now reconsidering it as costs rise.

Context: These are location- and time-specific opinions, not a required tariff. A higher price does not prove competence, and attendance after a fee increase is not guaranteed to recover in three months.

Question to investigate (editorial): What transparent fee balances clinical time, costs, affordability and assistance for patients who need it?

### Training & college checks

What must the department actually provide?

#### His pathway included overseas MBBS, teaching and several training changes

He describes overseas undergraduate study after unsuccessful Indian entry attempts, briefly taking pathology, teaching and writing a book before completing MD Medicine. He then left a short oncology super-specialty period after deciding he wanted his own work rather than another credential.

#### He strongly prioritises branch over institution

Using a marriage-venue analogy, he argues that a specialty remains with the doctor longer than the institution's name and advises choosing the preferred branch even at a less prestigious college.

#### New cases and integrated reading keep medicine interesting for him

He likes gaining some understanding across specialties and following basic science through to treatment. He describes repeated reading becoming rewarding and new cases prompting study after work rather than a monotonous routine.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [36:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2191s)

Context: Revenue is not net profit. The INR 15-20 lakh later scenarios are speculative, the timeline imprecise and no audited outcome distribution is offered.

Question to investigate (editorial): What remains after rent, staff, taxes, empty appointments and time for safe consultations?

#### He favours early consistent practice, with a long development horizon

He recommends beginning once suitably qualified and permitted, perhaps combining compatible work, because trust and visibility take years. He predicts growing OPD numbers and much higher daily receipts over five to ten years.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [39:07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2347s)

Context: Time alone does not assure 30-35 patients or INR 70,000-80,000 daily receipts. Government/private employment restrictions vary, and receipts are not salary or net profit.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do your contract, registration, supervision and continuity arrangements permit the proposed practice?

#### His own patient acquisition relied on online visibility and local signs

He says Google advertising and nearby signs brought more patients than a listing platform or his wider social-media audience at that time. He values local discoverability and consistent presence.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [40:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2414s)

Context: Personal ad performance is not general marketing evidence; professional advertising, testimonials, signage permissions and privacy rules require current review.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which lawful, ethical ways can accurately tell local patients about your service?

#### Startup-cost and property claims need an actual budget

He lists rent, deposits, furniture and fit-out, and suggests sharing space with similar-minded doctors to spread costs. He favours ownership when funds permit and even mentions a home room.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [41:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2500s)

Context: Several costs and the total are corrupted in captions, so no exact startup estimate is retained. Property is not guaranteed to appreciate or avoid loss, and home clinics require compliance.

Question to investigate (editorial): What complete local budget includes approvals, equipment, staff, accessibility, insurance and working capital?

#### Attracting other clinicians involves different risk preferences

He describes offering chambers but finding some doctors wanted a minimum guarantee rather than taking all risk from patient fees. Some stayed briefly and left, which made multispecialty expansion difficult.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [44:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2678s)

Context: Different preference for guaranteed pay is not a professional failing. Fee-sharing and allied income arrangements require legal and ethical review.

Question to investigate (editorial): What written partnership, sessional or employment structure shares risk and responsibility fairly?

#### He separates volatile daily visits from hoped-for break-even

He contrasts days with two versus twelve patients and describes estimated rented-team break-even around six months, while recovering a purchased setup might take three to five years. He acknowledges that his own recovery may take about five years.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [46:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2766s)

Context: These are personal estimates with shifting definitions, not audited results or guaranteed payback. A lab-cost number in captions is ambiguous.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does break-even mean monthly operating costs, fit-out recovery or full capital and financing recovery?

#### A successful teaching partnership still ended after relocation

He recalls a coaching venture operating from 2017 to 2022 with a partner whose mindset and patience matched his. It closed after the partner moved abroad, illustrating dependence on personal circumstances as well as compatibility.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [47:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=2859s)

Context: Unverified commercial success claims do not establish a typical partnership return.

Question to investigate (editorial): Have partners agreed roles, investment, cover, conflict resolution and an exit plan?

#### He lowered his consultation fee to make repeat care more affordable

He recounts fees ranging from INR 300 to INR 1,000 across earlier locations and INR 500 at the newer clinic. He says a lower price felt more acceptable to returning patients and resisted copying a neighbouring surgeon's fee.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [50:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=3052s)

Context: Personal consultation prices are not market benchmarks; repeat attendance alone does not establish clinical benefit.

Question to investigate (editorial): What fair, transparent fee can sustain adequate consultation time and access?

#### Referral commissions and high drug margins create conflicts of interest

Asked about commissions, he claims labs may offer 30-40 percent and describes a poor personal experience with heavily discounted pharmacy products. He then says he prefers established brands.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [53:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=3184s)

Context: Commission percentages are unverified and not endorsed; referral kickbacks may breach professional rules. Anecdotes cannot establish that an entire manufacturing area or cheaper generics are ineffective.

Question to investigate (editorial): Are investigation and prescribing decisions independent of financial incentives and supported by quality-assured sources?

#### He supports fair consultation fees while describing his own affordability concerns

He thinks established doctors in Delhi or Mumbai may charge around INR 1500-2000 and should not automatically equate higher fees with greed. Yet he says he held his own consultation fee for eight years partly to retain access for lower-income patients and is now reconsidering it as costs rise.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [26:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=1583s)

Context: These are location- and time-specific opinions, not a required tariff. A higher price does not prove competence, and attendance after a fee increase is not guaranteed to recover in three months.

Question to investigate (editorial): What transparent fee balances clinical time, costs, affordability and assistance for patients who need it?

#### He suggests incremental fee review with actual practice data

The host asks how to overcome fear of criticism when raising fees. Vatsya recommends a gradual change once a practice has a patient base, using rising rent, salaries and operating costs to explain the decision. He sees pricing as an ordinary business responsibility.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [27:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=1666s)

Context: The patient-count thresholds and arithmetic are informal examples, not a validated pricing formula. Financial growth is not the only measure of a worthwhile practice.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I review costs and access effects rather than change prices from fear or comparison alone?

#### Starting pay examples depend on location and clinical responsibility

He quotes Mumbai SR pay around INR 80,000-1 lakh per month, Delhi roughly INR 1.2-1.5 lakh, corporate starting roles INR 1.5-2 lakh and a personal remote/rural offer of INR 2.5-3 lakh where ICU skills mattered. He declined that remote offer.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [36:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2164s)

Context: These are interview-time examples, not current national pay scales; the Delhi caption phrase is slightly malformed.

Question to investigate (editorial): What are the written terms for hours, ICU responsibility, take-home pay, housing and indemnity?

#### He did not experience medicine saturation; preferred location still matters

He reports no personal difficulty finding medicine work but acknowledges competition for premium metropolitan posts. He suggests smaller-city general practice may offer demand and income, while family resources, lifestyle preferences and superspecialty referral patterns can favor a metro.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [38:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2324s)

Context: Claims that medicine can always create a vacancy, smaller cities are calmer or other branches are saturated are opinions, not labor-market data.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which locations can I commit to, and what do recent graduates and actual vacancies there show?

#### Setup budgets are rough startup estimates, not operating profit calculations

For a rented Mumbai clinic of about 500-600 square feet he sketches a deposit and basic examination equipment, estimating INR 5-6 lakh to start or INR 10-15 lakh for a premium setup. The host suggests smaller cities might cost half and he agrees without itemization.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [49:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2986s)

Context: These are not property purchase prices, verified current quotes or complete recurring-cost budgets. The smaller-city discount is speculative.

Question to investigate (editorial): What are my itemized capital and working-capital costs, including months of low attendance?

#### Lab and pharmacy arrangements create conflicts to examine

He describes laboratories or pharmacies offering consultation space and a 50/50 lab-profit-sharing scenario, while acknowledging limited knowledge of pharmacy margins. The host explicitly asks about commissions.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [51:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=3091s)

Context: Reporting arrangements is not endorsement or proof of legality. Check current professional rules on referral fees, ownership, disclosure and gifts; receipts and profit differ.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can my practice sustain independent, justified referrals and transparent billing without commissions?

#### She reports heavy admission and revenue pressure on some young consultants

She describes threats of job loss if admission, ICU or revenue expectations were not met, and says she knows physicians who left corporate employment, some for teaching or educational apps. She frames the clinician's primary duty as patient welfare rather than revenue generation.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [19:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=1164s)

Context: This is an attributed account, not evidence that every private hospital behaves this way or that all doctors are free of conflicts. No representative compensation comparison is provided.

Question to investigate (editorial): What incentives, admission expectations and protections for clinical autonomy are written into an offer?

#### She favours starting a clinic early while respecting competence and contracts

She calls private practice a long-term process that may begin with very few patients and suggests part-time evening OPD alongside paid work when the contract allows it. She favours beginning early rather than expecting immediate attendance.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [37:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=2270s)

Context: Earlier is not always safer or better. Clinical competence, registration, facility requirements, fatigue, household needs and employer rules still apply, and growth is not guaranteed.

Question to investigate (editorial): Am I clinically ready, contractually permitted and financially prepared for a gradual start?

### Culture, safety & ethics

What support, safeguards and professional boundaries matter?

#### Competing expectations and emotional depletion can create isolation

He describes being judged for earning, charging, buying things or not earning enough, then using much of his emotional energy with seriously ill patients and families. At home he may struggle to listen well, and nonmedical friends may assume a doctor cannot be distressed.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [17:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=1043s)

Context: These are personal and broad impressions, not comparative loneliness prevalence. A career setback does not mean lifelong depression, and seeking mental-health care should not be stigmatized.

Question to investigate (editorial): What peer, family and professional support would help me recover and communicate after difficult work?

#### Word of mouth is a meaningful feedback signal for him

He says he still works long days because seeing patients is satisfying, especially when a new patient comes on the recommendation of someone who improved. He treats this as a sign his work made a difference.

Dr Shubham Vatsya, a gastroenterologist, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [43:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fmheqgowBCM&t=2608s)

Context: Patient referrals and satisfaction do not by themselves establish treatment efficacy. Personal enjoyment does not make fourteen-hour days safe or necessary for others.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which parts of clinical work would remain rewarding after the novelty fades?

#### Emotional restraint, a mental-health break and a return to residency

He rejects the idea that doctors become heartless, saying restrained behavior can coexist with guilt and distress. He recalls a seven-day break when he considered quitting and family encouraged him to return, then celebrates his marriage and urges sincere work.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [57:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=3425s)

Context: Showing emotion is not proof of guilt or weakness. His return after apologizing is one story, not a rule to remain in harmful conditions.

Question to investigate (editorial): How will I recognize distress early and seek help without equating endurance with success?

#### She encounters age and gender assumptions from some patients

She perceives some older patients as less comfortable with a young woman physician and some younger patients as more able to relate and open up.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [54:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=3249s)

Context: Her patient-age pattern is not a universal rule. Bias is not evidence about actual competence or grounds to stereotype older patients.

Question to investigate (editorial): How does the institution support clinicians facing discrimination while maintaining respectful patient communication?

#### Internal medicine can involve repeated grief and abrupt emotional transitions

She says attachment develops through repeated rounds and contact with patients and families. Breaking news of a death can bring the doctor close to tears. She describes moving between terminal illness, family worries and obstetric critical-care situations within the same working day.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [27:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=1650s)

Context: These are personal experiences, not evidence that all clinicians react the same way or that visible emotion proves ethical care. Support and boundaries matter alongside empathy.

Question to investigate (editorial): How do I respond to emotional uncertainty, and what supervision, peer support and recovery would I need?

#### Cost-conscious investigation must not become undertesting

He argues that unnecessary expensive testing can deter patients and prefers a diagnosis-and-treatment approach with minimal investigation costs. He links this to the popularity of some local practitioners.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [52:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=3138s)

Context: Do not omit necessary investigation to retain patients, or infer qualified scope from popularity. Professional registration and evidence-based care remain essential.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which tests are clinically indicated, and how can costs be discussed without compromising diagnostic safety?

#### Alleged pressure for tests raises questions about clinical independence

Asked why some metropolitan corporates prefer DNB, he suggests familiarity with corporate systems and communication, then alleges that some hospitals encourage extensive investigations and treatments for insured patients. He contrasts this with resource-limited government care.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [27:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=1651s)

Context: These are allegations about some settings, not findings about named hospitals or evidence that a degree predicts ethics.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can doctors decline tests without a sound indication, and who reviews financial incentives?

#### Listening and affordability are central to his practice model

He emphasizes greeting patients, detailed history, listening and tailoring investigations to need and affordability. He sees useful public content as a way to become familiar, but says excessive investigations undermine outpatient practice.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [47:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=2845s)

Context: Informal medication comments are not prescribing advice. Patient preference does not replace evidence-based care; visibility is not competence.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I explain uncertainty and medication use, and build trust without overtesting or overselling?

#### She sees a continuing role for coordinated generalist care

She challenges using GP as a disparaging label and describes older patients frustrated by fragmented multispecialty visits. She expects broad coordinated care to become more valuable.

Dr Sanshriti Chauhan, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [11:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MSDg48V25_g&t=705s)

Context: An MD physician and an MBBS general practitioner are not identical qualifications. Her two-decade forecast and legal restrictions are not verified policy, and some referrals are necessary for safe care rather than needless fragmentation.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would I enjoy integrating multiple problems and coordinating specialist input?

#### She says she left a hospital on the first day over inappropriate ICU use

She alleges patients without clinical need were placed or retained in ICU to increase bills, contrary to her judgement as treating physician. She gives a mild diarrhoea/stomach-pain scenario without dehydration or comorbidity as an illustration and says she could not work in that system.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [5:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=328s)

Context: This is her unverified account of an unnamed workplace, not a proven finding or a rule for deciding ICU need from a short symptom description. Do not attach the story to hospital chains mentioned only as comparisons.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I review admission criteria and raise concerns about care driven by financial rather than clinical need?

#### A mismatch between her rounds and later care led her to question the system

She says evening rounds revealed that instructions such as catheter removal or transfer out of ICU had not been followed, and an MO attributed changes to management. The host asks whether a senior clinician might have had a different medical view. She emphasizes specialty competence and says a previous, much older physician reported leaving for similar reasons; she did not directly discuss the issue with management.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [7:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=479s)

Context: These are attributed accounts without records or the other party's response. Seniority alone does not determine correctness, but multidisciplinary disagreement can be legitimate and needs clinical review rather than assumptions.

Question to investigate (editorial): How are disagreements, order changes and responsibility documented and reviewed by the relevant treating team?

#### She distinguishes a beneficial referral from a paid referral cut

Asked about referral cuts, she gives the example of a senior dermatologist referring cosmetic procedures to her dermatologist husband without commission, aiming for good care and price for the patient. She argues a referral can be ethical and useful without financial inducement.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [13:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=801s)

Context: Her family example is not an independent audit and does not establish what proportion of referrals involve payments. A good referral is not made unethical simply because a patient changes doctors.

Question to investigate (editorial): Are referral reasons, alternatives and any relationships transparent and clinically justified?

#### She says unnecessary interventions are not limited to large hospitals

She mentions pressure to give IV fluids or admit people who might be managed otherwise and also criticizes unqualified providers selling drips or sugary energy products. The host argues he tends to assume a doctor is recommending care in good faith; she says ordinary patients often arrive with more suspicion.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [20:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=1244s)

Context: Examples lack enough detail to judge individual cases. Assumed good intentions do not prove appropriateness, and a patient's questions remain legitimate.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I explain why a proposed intervention is needed, what alternatives exist and when watchful care is safe?

#### Patients' suspicion can be tiring, but informed questions need respect

She recounts a febrile patient questioning typhoid testing and the host describes frustration when a normal ECG is treated as money wasted. They joke that repeated suspicion could tempt an ethical doctor to take cuts anyway. The underlying issue is how to communicate the purpose of testing and cope with mistrust.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [22:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=1356s)

Context: A normal test does not prove it was necessary, and these anecdotes do not establish indications. The retaliatory idea of misconduct is not endorsed: distrust never justifies unnecessary tests or referral payments.

Question to investigate (editorial): How can I explain pretest reasoning, uncertainty, cost and the value of a normal result without becoming defensive?

#### Uncertain prognosis requires goals-of-care discussions and careful consent

They discuss a ventilated patient after stroke, uncertain chances of recovery, high costs and family distress. Kaur describes discussing end-stage illness and DNI/DNR options rather than promising survival. The host argues that a poor outcome alone does not prove the care was exploitative.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [25:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=1524s)

Context: The anecdotal daily charge is not a fee schedule and no survival percentage is validated. DNI, DNR and withdrawal are distinct; decisions involve capacity, patient wishes, appropriate surrogates, clinical standards and current law, not an unrestricted family choice or blame.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does a unit provide documented prognosis discussions, treatment goals, palliative support and transparent costs?

#### She wants clear consultation boundaries and recognition of cognitive work

She recounts a couple trying to ask about laser treatment without a consultation fee and relatives expecting free advice. She argues assessment, explanations and recommendations are professional work even when nothing physical changes hands, and recommends clear communication by staff about fees.

Dr Prableen Kaur with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; Hindi/English captions paraphrased into English without independent diarization · [39:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TTOYPWT2N5U&t=2360s)

Context: This is her account of a disputed encounter, not the other party's perspective. General social contact is not automatically chargeable; urgent-care duties, accessibility, patient dignity and privacy still matter. Public anecdotes must be deidentified.

Question to investigate (editorial): Are fees, included services, follow-up terms and options for hardship explained before a consultation?

#### His diploma advice requires qualification-specific verification

He suggests a shorter recognised diploma may appeal to someone planning to join a family service, while MD/DNB and post-diploma DNB may better support some employment or academic aims.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [15:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=913s)

Context: The interview mixes branches and pathways. Do not assume a general-medicine diploma exists or that two years provide identical competence; current NMC/NBEMS eligibility governs.

Question to investigate (editorial): Is the exact diploma offered in the specialty, recognised for your aim, and eligible for the next training step?

#### He acknowledges toxic hierarchies while explaining them through service pressure

He reports intimidating seniors and indifferent faculty, linking conflict to patient volume, frustrated seniors and incomplete junior work. He also generalizes about younger residents wanting an easy escape; that is his interpretation rather than an established cause.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [12:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=768s)

Context: Workload and generational stereotypes do not excuse abuse; a famous name does not prove a toxic culture.

Question to investigate (editorial): How does this department distinguish fair accountability from humiliation or harassment?

#### Preparation can help learning but does not resolve unequal power

He describes anticipating questions, documenting cases and reporting accurately to avoid conflict. He initially suggests minimizing leave and keeping guides satisfied because of perceived examination influence, while saying DNB external assessment reduced local dependence.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [13:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=827s)

Context: These are survival strategies, not endorsement of favoritism or unsafe presenteeism. He describes his own training as DNB despite the MD title/introduction.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I ask questions and obtain feedback without surrendering rest or entitled leave?

#### Early complaints, boundaries and breaks are also part of his advice

He then advises resisting unreasonable demands, raising problems early and escalating harmful behavior to HOD or dean. Seniors should treat juniors as people, and severely distressed residents should prioritize wellbeing even if a break delays completion.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [16:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=1015s)

Context: His suggestion to leave without sanctioned leave reflects distress, not individualized employment advice. Seek support and safe handover where possible.

Question to investigate (editorial): What confidential support, independent grievance route and emergency leave arrangements exist?

#### COVID deaths and dismissive attitudes illustrate emotional strain

He recalls repeated ICU deaths during COVID and administrators dismissing requests for rest by comparing current shifts with older 24-36-hour duties. This bleak experience contrasts with his earlier hope that leaders now take mental health more seriously.

Dr Vishal Gabale, with questions and challenges from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [19:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i7Ba0B0Ob0s&t=1149s)

Context: His broad Indian-versus-Western hours comparison is not a verified roster or international standard.

Question to investigate (editorial): Are protected rest, debriefing and confidential mental-health care actually available?

#### Referral commissions and high drug margins create conflicts of interest

Asked about commissions, he claims labs may offer 30-40 percent and describes a poor personal experience with heavily discounted pharmacy products. He then says he prefers established brands.

Dr Aman Setiya; host questions and agreement distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [53:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=50QQrZnicLE&t=3184s)
