He describes moments of wanting to abandon the route after poor tests and relying on family, friends and mentors to share frustration before returning to preparation.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [15:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=943s)

Context: His suggestion of briefly venting then resuming is personal, not a time limit on distress or a substitute for mental-health care.

Question to investigate (editorial): Who can help me interpret setbacks and notice when stress needs more support?

#### He rejects a universal daily study-hours target

Prashanth reports flexible days ranging from no study to eight or ten hours and says he did not follow a sixteen-hour routine. He emphasizes revisions, planning, starting background and individual capacity.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [20:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1234s)

Context: Reported hours and statements about intelligence or stream-based effort are personal impressions, not validated requirements.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does my plan measure useful learning and recovery rather than only time at a desk?

#### He spent more time reviewing solutions than completing mock papers

He reports attempting as many as three papers a day, compressing solving time and spending longer on solutions, and roughly ten thousand practice questions overall. He describes becoming overly preoccupied with options.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [24:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1480s)

Context: His intense numbers are not a required minimum. Casual words such as paranoid or delusional do not establish a diagnosis; severe distress should not be normalized as necessary for success.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do I understand why answers are right and wrong, and is my practice volume sustainable?

#### Flexible targets and revision worked around internship duties

He describes naps after duty, flexible study windows and a focus on completing subjects rather than rigid weekly schedules, reporting an average six to seven hours. He delayed most MCQ mocks until close to prelims and otherwise read and revised.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [33:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=2000s)

Context: Reported study hours are not a prescription to sacrifice sleep. His unusual MCQ timing is personal and may not suit another candidate.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can my plan remain realistic through heavy postings and preserve sleep and clinical responsibilities?

### Future & claims to verify

Which expectations need current evidence?

#### He says civil service attracted him rather than dissatisfaction pushing him out of medicine

He describes interest in humanities, current affairs, variety and dynamic work. Resource constraints in patient care made him think about a different systems-level impact, while he explicitly says doctors' direct contribution is also substantial.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [17:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=1075s)

Context: Administrative roles also have constraints and do not automatically offer greater impact or satisfaction than clinical work. This is his personal motivation.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which specific responsibilities attract me to administration, beyond status or escape?

#### He uses prevention and vaccine access to illustrate a different type of public impact

He contrasts much clinical curative work with administrative opportunities to reduce upstream risks and improve access, using cervical-cancer prevention and HPV vaccination as an example.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [19:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=1146s)

Context: Clinicians also deliver prevention and public-health work, and administrators do not act alone. The example is a career illustration, not a clinical vaccination protocol.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do I enjoy organizing systems, prevention and resource access as much as individual diagnosis and treatment?

#### He spent time understanding the actual exam before committing to the switch

He says the decision developed over roughly a year, with online information helping him identify the syllabus, stages, optional subject and resources. By medical college's third year he felt clearer about pursuing this route.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [20:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=1213s)

Context: Online accounts can democratize access but need checking against current official notifications. His timing need not be optimal for every candidate.

Question to investigate (editorial): Have I investigated the daily work, entry process, opportunity cost and fallback options of the alternative?

#### He navigated family hopes for postgraduate medicine while avoiding a decision driven by sunk costs

He reiterates that the move was driven by attraction to civil service, not being fed up with medical study. Family initially preferred completing PG but ultimately supported him, while some relatives continued suggesting another medical exam.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [26:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=1569s)

Context: His supportive circumstances are a meaningful advantage. Neither staying because of prior investment nor switching early is universally correct.

Question to investigate (editorial): How would I discuss a career change, its risks and its funding with people who support me?

#### He obtained a service in the first attempt and prepared again while in training

He clarifies that the first attempt led to DANICS through a reserve list, even though his name was absent from the first main list. He sought IAS for a broader field role and says he continued preparation without first resigning from the service.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [35:47](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=2147s)

Context: The host's framing of leaving a service is corrected by the guest. Attempt, service-allocation, leave and repeat-exam rules change and require current official verification.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can a secure current role coexist with preparation under the rules that apply to me?

#### He expects constraints and coordination between administrative and political roles

He describes balancing stakeholders and taking principled decisions within political and administrative structures. He says decision authority varies by issue and level and that both sides need coordination.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [57:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=3468s)

Context: The account simplifies legal powers and does not establish a universal division of authority or prove that improper pressure never occurs. Check actual service rules and context.

Question to investigate (editorial): Would I tolerate negotiation, constrained authority and responsibility to multiple stakeholders?

#### He argues that a medical graduate need not be confined to one conventional clinical career

He wants credible avenues into administration, policy, politics and other interests, saying an early decision to study biology need not define every later career choice. He recognizes that different work may fit a person better.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [1:04:31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=3871s)

Context: Alternative interests are not automatic job offers. Qualifications, funding, entry competition and professional scope still require specific investigation.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which realistic roles match my abilities, values and constraints, and what additional training do they need?

#### Medical interest and administrative ambition coexisted before graduation

Prashanth says he had considered civil services before class twelve but chose MBBS from genuine medical interest. Exposure to insurance and government health schemes, especially around COVID, reinforced his wish to contribute through administration; he also credits his grandmother's service outlook.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [7:51](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=471s)

Context: The contrast between treating dozens and impacting millions is illustrative rhetoric; signatures do not guarantee beneficial implementation, and clinical careers can also affect systems.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do I want clinical relationships, system-level policy work, or another combination of public service?

#### Interest, prior examples and effort helped him change subject domains

He acknowledges that transitioning into general studies was difficult despite sounding effortless in hindsight. He names earlier medical graduates as inspiration, admits geography remained weak, and describes avoiding another prelims cycle as a motivator.

#### His advice to sit prelims depends on remaining attempts and readiness

He discourages skipping early attempts solely through fear while acknowledging more caution near a final attempt. He regards fear as recurring across prelims, mains and interview.

#### PG remained a fallback despite an available NEET-PG rank

He reports a roughly 5000 NEET-PG rank and says PG was a fallback. His mother gave him freedom to choose; friends were confident, while some professors and alumni preferred clinical or US training. He notes that medical graduates can also struggle for jobs.

Question to investigate (editorial): What fallback is feasible, and can I discuss my choice with supporters without confusing support with certainty?

#### A medical background informs his aspiration to improve systems

He mentions anatomy as a subject he feared, then explains that a doctor-administrator perspective might help identify system deficiencies and contribute to change rather than simply leaving disliked training.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [28:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1718s)

Question to investigate (editorial): Which problems do I want to work on, and what role actually has the skills and authority to address them?

#### Medical science optional fit his strong existing preparation

He chose medical science through a cost-benefit judgement, drawing on a strong MBBS base and concise notes so he could focus on general studies. He reports only fifteen to twenty days across the year for optional revision and recommends it to those confident in the subjects.

### Shared training and wider residency discussion

These are general preparation or training discussions, not findings about the specialty as a whole.

#### Interest and supportive family mattered within a narrow local picture of available careers

He describes a small-town upbringing where medicine and engineering were the most visible options. He developed curiosity about biology and later broader academic interests while receiving family and friend support.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [3:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=234s)

Context: One personal background does not describe all small-town students or guarantee that interest alone removes access barriers.

#### He recalls a strongly positive undergraduate experience at AIIMS Jodhpur

He calls his medical-college years one of the best phases of his life and credits faculty, staff, friends, seniors, classes, sport and festivals. He sees the eventual institution as a positive outcome despite earlier preference for Delhi.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [5:21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=321s)

Context: This is an undergraduate recollection, not a current postgraduate safety audit or a rebuttal of other residents' experiences. Different roles, departments and periods can produce different accounts.

#### He entered medicine through biology interest and coaching partly shaped by information gaps

He describes a family engineer/doctor pattern as a lighthearted influence but says biology curiosity was primary. Lack of medical-career guidance and proximity made Kota coaching seem the obvious entrance route.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [7:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=437s)

Context: The coaching decision reflects his period and resources; it is not evidence that relocation or a specific commercial provider is necessary.

#### He acknowledges coaching pressure while saying that environment worked for him personally

He describes constant visibility of competitors as a source of pressure but says the structure matched his own strategy. He now considers online resources a viable reason not to assume everyone must move to a coaching city.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [8:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=492s)

Context: His success cannot establish the safest or most effective setting for someone else. Online availability also does not guarantee access, quality or support.

#### They discuss vulnerable students and the need for reliable exam administration

He calls reported student deaths a grim reality and worries about very early, prolonged preparation and high-pressure examinations. He argues that an administration responsible for many futures needs due diligence and reliable logistics.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [9:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=580s)

#### He credits mentors who supported curiosity and emphasized empathy toward patients

He recalls a teacher responding kindly to uncertainty and encouraging discussion of civil-service interests. He also recounts a lesson about listening to patients and attendants and retaining altruism, empathy or at least sympathy.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [15:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=914s)

Context: Names, wording and encounters are personal recollections, not a current faculty evaluation. Empathy complements clinical competence, boundaries and professional duties.

#### He admires junior residents' diligence while recognizing severe personal costs

Reflecting on internship, he describes first-year postgraduate residents as exceptionally busy, with personal time and mental and physical health affected. He sees commitment as a lesson but later explicitly calls for better balance.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [16:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=999s)

#### He used syllabus overlap but prioritized completing medical training responsibly

With medical science as an optional subject, he studied overlapping topics in depth while respecting final-year exams and internship duties. He rejects skipping internship simply because he did not plan a clinical career.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [21:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=1296s)

#### Small regular study periods and a planned gap were more realistic than doing everything at once

He says some days permitted a few hours after duty and rest, while intensive postings did not. He accepted that full preparation might require time after internship rather than expect an immediate result.

#### He separates preparation from the uncertainty of obtaining a particular top rank

Context: Composure is not a moral test, and significant anxiety may need professional support. A flow-state anecdote is not a reliable method for everyone.

#### A weaker second result led him to practice expressing knowledge, not simply accumulating it

He reports a lower second-attempt score despite more study and attributes part of the gap to insufficient answer-writing practice. In the third attempt he focused on clear, structured responses.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [43:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=2613s)

Context: Score differences and causes are his retrospective interpretation, not a controlled comparison. Examination performance also includes factors outside an individual's control.

#### He prepared for another attempt before the previous cycle's final result

He explains that the long exam cycle can leave little time before the next preliminary paper and says he continued preparation while waiting. After disappointment he used an identified writing gap to refocus, with less social activity for a period.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [45:09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=2709s)

Context: Dates and intervals are approximate historical accounts. Hope for the best and prepare for the worst does not mean indefinitely postponing review, rest or alternative work.

#### A rescue scenario taught him to integrate his medical background into situational answers

He recounts an interview question in which his first answer emphasized official rescue and investigation but omitted what he, as a doctor, might contribute immediately. He links the feedback to presence of mind and realistic situational thinking.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [48:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=2888s)

Context: The recalled scenario is not an emergency-care protocol. Scene safety, calling appropriate help, assessment and indication matter; CPR is not automatically given to every person in a rescue situation.

#### He recommends genuine responses and acknowledging when recall fails

He discusses unexpected analogies, a historical quotation about doctors and medical questions including cancer care. He says it is better to admit that one cannot recall something than invent an answer.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [51:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=3103s)

Context: Recalled questions and quotations may be imperfect, and a single interview story cannot predict a future panel. Do not use his medical examples as treatment guidance.

#### His interview examples connect medicine with health policy and public accountability

He recalls being questioned on pandemic response, private/public disparities and allegations of profiteering. He says an answer should be a reasoned personal perspective rather than a claim that only he could solve a complex problem.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [52:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=3153s)

Context: These are recalled interview themes, not an independent evaluation of pandemic policy or proof of wrongdoing by any institution.

#### He explicitly calls for safe workplaces and better postgraduate duty arrangements

He prioritizes safety for doctors, especially outside protected institutions, and says work-life balance in PG has been neglected. He rejects expecting someone to work like a horse or assuming thirty-six-hour duties must continue.

Dr Anuj Agnihotri, with questions from host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [1:03:46](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E8anEOf9yd8&t=3826s)

Context: His positive perception of safety in his institution is personal and not a current guarantee. This reform stance should be retained alongside his earlier admiration for overworked residents.

#### MBBS written exams gave him a perceived advantage in mains

He disagrees that medicine offers no transferable skills, crediting experience writing structured subjective answers, especially medal exams, while describing prelims as his greater difficulty.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [17:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1049s)

Context: His strengths do not imply all medical graduates can postpone answer-writing preparation.

#### He distinguishes a real interview from cinematic dramatization

Asked about the film 12th Fail, he says seating may resemble the depiction but the real board can encourage conversation, including Hindi or regional-language arrangements rather than the film's dramatic conflict.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [25:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1526s)

Context: One candidate's impression is not a guarantee about every panel; interpreter and language rules require official checking.

#### The host and guest discuss overwork, low pay and resident mental health

The host raises long resident duties, underpayment and violence. Prashanth describes student advocacy with IMA and NMC and perceived progress on mental health; the host calls for limits on thirty-six- and forty-eight-hour work periods.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [30:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1833s)

Context: Reported NMC notifications and the figure of 37000 affected students are unverified here and may conflate surveyed respondents with diagnosed illness. No actual stipend schedule is given.

#### They call for durable protection from violence and exam-policy stability

They advocate stronger, lasting protection for healthcare workers rather than relying on emergency-era provisions, and ask for more stability around NEET-PG and NExT.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [32:01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1921s)

Context: A demand for a central law does not prove it has passed. Current legal protections and examination policy need official sources.

#### Warm peer bonds do not justify ragging or coercion

He warmly recalls seniors and juniors, helping with medal exams and attending family events, then calls some unreported ragging memories positive and says physical abuse is the limit.

Dr Prashanth with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [33:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=G_aUApA71uI&t=1980s)

Context: The interview gives no details allowing the claimed activities to be assessed. Nonphysical humiliation, intimidation, sexual coercion and forced participation can also be abuse; consent and dignity matter even when someone later recalls friendship.

#### Limited resources and conceptual understanding formed his core method

He worked around light and heavy internship postings, used few resources per subject and emphasized concepts, analysis and lessons from earlier competitive examinations rather than memorizing everything.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [11:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=701s)

Context: One successful candidate cannot establish that the same resource volume or preparation plan will work for others.

#### Mains required speed, presentation and physical stamina

Bansal describes successive written papers as tiring, including hand pain. He practiced recognizing question demands, presenting answers clearly and completing papers in time.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [12:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=739s)

Context: Pain is not a required badge of commitment; breaks, ergonomics and appropriate care remain relevant.

#### Unexpected interview order tested composure and honesty

He expected time to settle at the interview venue but was called first after delayed formalities. He recounts saying he did not know the first answer, staying calm, and seeing the process as a test of judgement, ethics and teamwork as well as knowledge; he reports a 209 score.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [14:41](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=881s)

Context: His interpretation and score are self-report; calmness alone does not guarantee selection.

#### Interview questions connected medicine with economics, technology and society

His recalled questions ranged across Bhutan, hydropower, Manipur, spurious drugs, pharmaceutical exports, US tariffs and WHO, nationalism, a temple, electrolytes and school boards. He argues that admitting uncertainty is preferable to inventing answers.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [18:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=1122s)

Context: This is recalled interview content, not an authenticated question bank. The electrolyte-fruit question is not clinical advice; no treatment recommendation follows from it.

#### He distinguishes prelims qualification from ranked written preparation

He says prelims marks did not determine his final rank and describes short notes keyed to the published mains syllabus, updated with current affairs.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [35:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=2105s)

Context: Exam rules and current syllabus require official checking; the interview alone is not an application guide.

#### He proposes duty limits, compulsory rest and practical skill training

His first proposed health-system reforms are caps on resident duty time, protected recovery and greater attention to practical clinical skills, because exam preparation can displace bedside learning.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [35:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=2154s)

Context: These are proposed reforms, not a claim that the protections already operate in every hospital.

#### Safety requires security, enforcement and better communication

He proposes implementing laws against violence, improving hospital security and CCTV, and better doctor-patient communication while recognizing overwork and frustration.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [38:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=2285s)

Context: Communication problems never justify assault. Security must be trained, lawful and respectful; the interview does not establish that guards alone prevent violence.

#### He proposes accountable complaints rather than repeating toxic hierarchies

For resident mistreatment, he suggests a committee where juniors can raise grievances and transparent follow-up that tracks resolution, alongside a positive learning environment instead of reproducing what seniors suffered.

Dr Pulkit Bansal with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia; captions paraphrased without independent diarization · [39:00](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OXhYJR1YCqc&t=2340s)

Context: A committee on paper is insufficient without confidentiality, protection against retaliation and fair independent processes.

#### Liking biology and enjoying clinical practice are different

Shivin enjoyed biology but says hospital work and patient care did not engage him. Model UN, youth parliament, international relations and a college debating society helped him recognise other interests.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [2:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=143s)

Context: His lack of clinical interest is personal; it does not establish that medicine is less varied or worthwhile.

#### Choosing outside the usual postgraduate path

With supportive doctor parents, he explored UPSC while most medical classmates prepared for postgraduate entrance. He recalls feeling excluded by clinical conversations and affected by peer judgement.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [3:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=235s)

Context: Recollections concern his own cohort and do not establish the culture of every medical college.

#### He revises the wish to prove superiority

He acknowledges once wanting civil-service success to prove himself to medical peers, then explicitly rejects the idea that one occupation makes someone superior. He questions a narrow UG-to-PG-to-superspecialty ladder.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [6:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=372s)

Context: His allegation that faculty discouraged an IAS session is unverified historical recollection; no occupation is inherently superior.

#### Leaving a secure path needs a positive reason

He describes leaving a comparatively secure medical trajectory because of genuine lack of interest and attraction to varied administrative work.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [7:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=446s)

Context: Medicine also includes public health, research, teaching and administration; his comparison should not reduce it to treating one patient at a time.

#### Explore alternatives while protecting medical training

He began exploring in third year, spoke with officials through family contacts, sampled coaching and paused for final medical examinations. He recalls nearly failing a practical, then failing his first UPSC attempt and succeeding later; he generally favours serious preparation after internship.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [9:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=543s)

Context: Family access and his preparation sequence are not universally available. Check current examination eligibility and official notices rather than relying on the interview.

#### Develop interests without turning learning into a status contest

He recommends cultivating general awareness and describes using political knowledge to respond to peers who belittled his medical knowledge.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [10:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=635s)

Context: His political examples require independent checking; knowing trivia does not compensate for unsafe clinical competence.

#### He explicitly acknowledges the privilege behind career risks

He taught around his UPSC preparation, sampled LBSNAA and service training, and eventually preferred teaching. He explicitly credits financial and parental support that made switching possible, contrasting it with his father's need for security.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [16:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1019s)

Context: Do not universalise the ability to leave a secure role or infer that enthusiasm alone pays for a transition.

#### Inspect the eventual job before buying preparation

He describes months of exploration before committing and recommends speaking to working professionals and understanding the destination rather than pursuing examination prestige.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [19:17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1157s)

Context: Access to officials through family contacts shaped his exploration; seek multiple independent accounts.

#### Test genuine curiosity with independent reading

Reading polity and history, constitutional debates and related material helped him test his interest before or alongside formal courses.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [20:49](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1249s)

#### Study stamina does not make UPSC a guaranteed switch

He believes medical training can build study stamina and suggests a bounded preparation period and considering medical science as an optional subject when suitable.

#### A medical degree is not an automatic fallback plan

His own alternatives included medical-tourism liaison at a hospital where his father worked, teaching and healthcare management. He corrects the suggestion that the hospital belonged to his father.

#### Budget for the examination cycle as well as preparation

He describes current affairs, guidance and the long sequence of preparation and examination stages, using a hypothetical preparation year followed by an examination-cycle year.

He recalls anxiety, an unfamiliar first question and discussion arising from his application details, preferences and international-relations diploma. He says he admitted not knowing.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [26:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1584s)

Context: One interview cannot predict another candidate's questions, assessment or result.

#### Practise presenting opposing arguments responsibly

He recounts an impromptu debate presenting arguments for and against a minimal state and a discussion of community institutions through his anthropology optional.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [27:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1677s)

#### Prepare claimed expertise and admit limits

He stresses integrity, careful wording and not pretending to know material, particularly subjects listed in the application.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [30:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1839s)

#### Choose preparation around interest and workable methods

He did not choose medical science as his optional because he did not enjoy it. He says effort and ability both matter, illustrating his view with informal percentages and reading arithmetic.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [31:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=1915s)

#### Therapy helped after failure and personal difficulties

He describes depression and anxiety after his first unsuccessful attempt and personal difficulties, compounded by comparison with earning peers. He sought a psychologist, found therapy helpful and credits supportive parents.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [33:56](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=2036s)

#### A successful selection need not settle long-term fit

He says leaving service was not simply disappointment at missing his first preference. He currently enjoys studying deeply and teaching, while acknowledging uncertainty about what he might have done in a different service.

Dr. Shivin, medical graduate, former civil-service trainee and UPSC teacher; host questions and guest recollections are distinguished. Mixed Hindi/English captions may contain transcription errors. · [35:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RmZqiq_iZ4I&t=2136s)

Context: His comments about further attempts and retaining service require checking against current age, attempt and employment rules.

#### Medical administration requires additional skills

Discussing a proposed Indian Medical Service, he is not opposed to doctors administering but argues that administration has its own skills and that doctors already lead many institutions.

Personal fit (editorial): What support, legal awareness and safety arrangements do I need in a workplace?

### Fit & daily work

Which parts of the actual work would I enjoy?

#### Personal experience helped him connect with trainees reporting problems

The host introduces him as a doctor who regularly raises medical-community issues online. Dhruv says he recognised parts of his own college experience in messages from students and residents and wanted their concerns to be heard beyond their institutions.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [2:22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=142s)

Context: A self-described motivation, not independent verification of every submitted complaint.

Question to investigate (editorial): What would motivate sustained advocacy, and what support and boundaries would I need?

#### Relatable medical humour became an entry point into public issues

He recalls making medically linked memes that spread among students and even appeared in teaching slides. During COVID-era reports of assault, people asked him to use that reach; he gradually expanded to harassment, internship and other workforce concerns.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [8:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=514s)

Context: Virality is a communication outcome, not proof that a claim is true or an intervention works.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can my communication format convey accurate context as well as connect with an audience?

#### He distinguishes his medical focus from broader political commentary

The host compares him with Dhruv Rathee. Dhruv says the other creator works across issues whereas his own focus is the medical community; he wants collective amplification to make authorities hear relevant problems.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [15:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=916s)

Question to investigate (editorial): Can collective advocacy amplify verified concerns while protecting affected people and avoiding pile-ons?

#### Language, reasoning and advocacy drew him toward law

He traces an early interest in advocacy to admiring Ram Jethmalani, then reflecting on his own language, memory and willingness to argue. The idea of a legal career emerged during medical school.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [5:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=312s)

Context: Admiration for a prominent professional is not evidence of a typical legal career.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which activities reveal sustained interest and strengths outside your current training?

#### Law felt like a more natural intellectual environment

He recalls greater enthusiasm and a sense of finding like-minded people after moving to law. This contrasts with his own medical-college experience rather than establishing a hierarchy between professions.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [9:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=574s)

Context: Retrospective satisfaction is personal and affected by the opportunities that followed.

Question to investigate (editorial): Where do you consistently enjoy the problems and conversations of the field?

#### Teaching means making difficult material understandable

He describes enjoying constitutional and legal teaching for UPSC learners from varied backgrounds. Reading judgments and Ambedkar informs his preparation, but he values understanding over memorisation; practice and teaching enrich each other.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [16:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=993s)

Context: His dual legal and teaching career is one model rather than a guaranteed pathway.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do you enjoy adapting difficult ideas for learners with different starting points?

#### He values stimulating peers, young learners and peaceful sleep

In rapid fire he enjoys intellectually sharp legal colleagues and remaining connected with younger learners. His definition of success combines security with sleeping peacefully; he credits his father and mentors.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [53:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=3208s)

Context: Retirement-money banter is personal aspiration, not financial guidance.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which combination of intellectual community, stability and personal values matters to you?

#### Becoming accustomed to threats does not eliminate their emotional cost

He describes a growing tolerance for online abuse but also a recent episode that disturbed his peace for several days. He sees emerging from difficult periods as building capacity to continue.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [13:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=830s)

### Shared training and wider residency discussion

These are general preparation or training discussions, not findings about the specialty as a whole.

#### Advocacy developed alongside a clinical career

Krishnan briefly describes medical school, postgraduate orthopaedic training, senior residency and overseas fellowships before explaining how working conditions drew him into representation.

Dr. Rohan Krishnan, orthopaedic surgeon and medical-rights advocate, and host Nachiket Bhatia. Cached captions are labelled Hindi but largely English; organisation names, medical terms and legal wording may be corrupted. · [2:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-GTsWXL_tGg&t=143s)

#### Ask about real hours and recovery, not only official rosters

He recalls continuous duties stretching across days, little time off, poor sleep and feeling physically unwell in first-year residency. Clearing the entrance examination did not create the life he expected.

Dr. Rohan Krishnan, orthopaedic surgeon and medical-rights advocate, and host Nachiket Bhatia. Cached captions are labelled Hindi but largely English; organisation names, medical terms and legal wording may be corrupted. · [3:57](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-GTsWXL_tGg&t=237s)

#### Resident representation can organise concerns and seek remedy

He says a conversation with a senior leader prompted him to examine rules, organise colleagues, pursue court action and build broader resident representation beyond Delhi.

Dr. Rohan Krishnan, orthopaedic surgeon and medical-rights advocate, and host Nachiket Bhatia. Cached captions are labelled Hindi but largely English; organisation names, medical terms and legal wording may be corrupted. · [5:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-GTsWXL_tGg&t=324s)

#### A delayed intake can affect the residents already working

Dr. Rohan Krishnan, orthopaedic surgeon and medical-rights advocate, and host Nachiket Bhatia. Cached captions are labelled Hindi but largely English; organisation names, medical terms and legal wording may be corrupted. · [11:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-GTsWXL_tGg&t=702s)

#### A hospital should provide safety during work and rest

Singh describes previously reassuring her family that reaching the hospital meant she was safe. The killing shook that assumption and prompted her to speak and protest.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [2:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=143s)

Context: This is her experience of fear and advocacy, not a measured comparison of hospital safety.

#### Understand the timing and limits of the account

She recalls learning about the death through student networks and joining protests soon afterwards. The discussion occurs roughly ten days into the protests.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [4:42](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=282s)

Context: Her account of messages and official handling is not independently verified. Later investigation and court findings must be checked separately.

#### Protection should preserve equal training opportunities

She rejects removing women from night duties as the answer to violence, arguing that safety measures should not become unequal access to work and training.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [5:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=328s)

Context: Do not blame the victim's location, clothing or shift. Any current duty rule must be verified through official policy.

#### Violence can change everyday confidence and trust

She describes more frequent location sharing and fear after dark, and recalls previously feeling safe with a colleague. She now finds trust harder.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [18:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1095s)

Context: Her distress should not become a claim that all men, colleagues or hospitals are dangerous.

#### Verify actual duties and protected recovery time

She reports extremely long continuous duties and describes reaching a point overnight when she needs sleep. The hosts treat such schedules as a major working-condition problem.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [22:33](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1353s)

Context: Reported hours are anecdotal and not a standard to normalise. Ask current residents and check written rules and compliance.

#### A proposed protection law is not a current legal entitlement

She advocates a central healthcare-worker protection measure and sketches proposed penalties, compensation and investigation provisions.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [23:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1390s)

Context: Her account of a proposal, dates, coverage and penalties is not verified legal advice. Confirm enacted law and current procedures from official sources.

#### The guest favours institutional security over arming doctors

Asked whether doctors should carry guns, Singh disagrees and favours security guards, surveillance and a rapid alarm and police-response system. She recounts colleagues hiding during an aggressive incident.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [26:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1565s)

Context: The event and response-time comparisons are unverified anecdotes. Surveillance must respect privacy; weapon proposals are not safety guidance.

#### Gender discrimination can enter the clinical workplace

She recounts alleged aggression after the birth of a girl and distress among mothers under family pressure, contrasting this with her joy at helping deliver a baby.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [27:03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1623s)

Context: The incidents are personal reports. A child's sex is no one's fault; do not redirect blame to either parent.

#### Fear of violence can influence career fit

The host describes a threatening crowd during an unsuccessful resuscitation in his internship and says it reinforced his move away from clinical work. He renews a gun proposal; the guest questions whether it would help.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [28:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1704s)

Context: This is one remembered incident and a personal decision, not a risk estimate for all branches. Death does not itself prove negligence, and armed confrontation is not endorsed.

#### Safe rest areas are an institutional responsibility

They reject criticism of a doctor for resting alone in a seminar room. Singh describes being so tired during night work that any available bed can seem welcome.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [31:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=1918s)

Context: The disputed remarks attributed to a particular official are unverified. The victim's decision to rest does not make her responsible for violence.

#### Accountability requires records and due process

They question administrative handling, family communication and a principal's reassignment. Singh later explicitly cautions that falsely framing someone would also be wrong and says investigators must determine responsibility.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [36:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2195s)

Context: Their account of court questions, transfers and statements is not verified. Preserve the guest's caution rather than presenting guilt as established.

#### Staff need safe reporting and representation

The conversation raises rumours of other misconduct and fears of intimidation through attacks, transfers or notices. The practical issue is whether trainees can report concerns without retaliation.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [37:20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2240s)

Context: Claims about particular officials, alleged illegal activity and motives for transfers or notices are not verified and should not be repeated as facts.

#### Collective action can bring solidarity and exhaustion

She describes a march and handmade rakhi campaign, alternating determination with helplessness, and reframes protection as a shared responsibility beyond one's own family.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [38:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2335s)

Context: Solidarity does not guarantee a legal outcome; participation should be voluntary and safe.

#### Inspect facilities for both residents and patients

She criticises old buildings, toilets, limited cooling and equipment and contrasts heavy hands-on exposure with inadequate manpower. She questions why poorer patients should receive less protected care.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [40:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2429s)

Context: Her descriptions are local and historical; do not generalise to all institutions in a state. Performing many procedures does not establish competence or justify insufficient supervision.

#### Resources need maintenance and accountable use

She calls for more investment in health and education and for funds and individual responsibilities to be monitored, while acknowledging that failure can occur at multiple levels.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [44:15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2655s)

Context: Her corruption examples are illustrative, not evidence that a particular employee or institution diverted funds.

#### Rest and staffing are patient-safety measures

They welcome the idea of shorter structured shifts and argue that fatigue reduces concentration and increases error risk.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [45:50](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2750s)

Context: The claimed first institution and specific shift policy are not independently verified. A nominal limit alone does not demonstrate compliance or adequate handover.

#### Protest decisions also affect patient access

She describes difficult decisions to withdraw services, redistribution of work and senior clinicians covering patients. She says patient suffering was distressing and their dispute was not with patients.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [46:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=2813s)

Context: Her assurance about coverage does not prove that no patient was harmed. Check current legal and professional requirements; this is not a recommendation to stop services.

#### Retain respect for patients alongside demands for safety

Asked whether India deserves doctors, Singh points to understanding patients as well as difficult encounters and asks for reciprocal empathy and practical change.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [51:52](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=3112s)

Context: A population does not earn or lose entitlement to care as a group; individual misconduct should not justify contempt or discrimination.

#### Teach consent and equality beyond warning girls

She favours teaching boys and girls equality, sharing domestic responsibilities, improving sex education and treating menstruation as ordinary biology. She recalls sexualised harassment while teaching online.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [55:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=3324s)

Context: Her retort to a student is an anecdote, not a recommended teaching method. Pornography, testosterone or social class do not provide a simple causal explanation for sexual violence.

#### Repeated advocacy can carry an emotional burden

She says repeatedly retelling the case reawakens pain. Both speakers urge broad solidarity across medical and nonmedical groups and describe local mobilisation.

Dr. Rakshita Singh, described as an intern in Kolkata and medical educator, and host Nachiket Bhatia. The guest is not an investigator or a verified eyewitness to the crime; later host monologue is identified separately. · [58:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Af4uAQM5aSY&t=3512s)

Context: Comparing one person's distress with another's should not invalidate either. Mobilisation claims are recollections, not a guarantee of justice.

#### He describes hierarchy and psychological harassment as recurring concerns

Asked for the most prominent toxic issue, he first notes that people experience harm differently, then points to senior-junior hierarchy and psychological mistreatment. He refers to reported serious cases across institutions and regions.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [4:28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=268s)

Context: Named incidents and links to deaths are not independently investigated here. Personal differences in distress do not make abuse acceptable or imply a single cause for suicide.

#### Paying seniors' personal bills is an abuse issue, not a training requirement

He describes complaints from Gujarat that juniors were expected to pay seniors' canteen expenses. He says publicity led to journalists, officials and college leadership acting, and claims the practice stopped in the institutions concerned.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [5:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=324s)

Context: The reported response and broad claim that the culture ended are not an independently verified current audit of Gujarat colleges.

#### Reported interventions offer hope without proving a universal rescue pathway

He says some highly distressed trainees found a voice and that action followed complaints at other colleges. The host praises even one life positively affected and encourages people with genuine concerns to seek help and reach authorities.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [6:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=394s)

Context: Claims of lives saved and colleges becoming toxicity-free are not measured outcomes. One social-media contact cannot guarantee timely crisis support or institutional action.

#### His NEET-UG account reflects an active historical controversy

He argues there was evidence of leaks and inconsistencies in official responses, referring to arrests, allegations beyond one locality and a pending July court hearing. He wants answers and accountability rather than announcements of another committee.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [17:30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=1050s)

Context: This is contemporaneous advocacy before the outcome, not a current judicial finding. Arrests, allegations and claimed confessions are not interchangeable with proven system-wide misconduct.

#### He makes a re-examination view conditional on the extent of the problem

Asked whether NEET should be repeated, he says a repeat would be warranted if the effects go beyond the cited candidate group and isolated incidents. He does not present an unconditional answer divorced from that premise.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [18:40](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=1120s)

Context: A policy opinion, not an examination directive or legal conclusion.

#### Last-minute postponement imposes both emotional and financial costs

He says he wants to consider more than one perspective, then strongly criticises very late NEET-PG cancellation and the absence of a clear new date. Examples include candidates waking to the news, interstate or overseas travel and hotel costs borne by families. He argues the organisers should be accountable for those expenses.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [19:13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=1153s)

Context: Specific examples and costs are not independently verified. His call for reimbursement is a proposed responsibility, not proof of a legal entitlement.

#### FMG discussion centres on extended training, uncertainty and respectful treatment

Host and guest criticise additional internship demands and describe protests, long waits and perceived disrespect at a regulator's office. Dhruv argues that some routes can become extremely long and asks for clearer accreditation and training rules.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [21:34](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=1294s)

Context: The three-year unpaid-internship and ten-year-degree examples are not universal FMG rules. The world-record remark is rhetorical, not a documented record.

#### Include affected clinicians when designing policy

They argue that FMGs need representation in decisions affecting FMGs and that repeated reversals create insecurity and consume time that could be spent training or working. They ask that unresolved groups, including some China-returned students, not be left out.

Dr Dhruv Chauhan, medical social-media creator and advocate; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [24:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tSAMkNzphR8&t=1465s)

Context: This is an argument for participatory policy, not proof that every disputed rule is invalid.

#### Violence and expectations of unpaid selflessness troubled him

The host raises fear of violence and litigation. Arora describes discomfort with expecting doctors to be selfless while denying them safety, respect and reasonable payment, and says this also influenced his departure.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [24:53](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=1493s)

Context: This is an attributed critique, not a measured estimate of violence or attitudes toward all doctors.

#### He argues existing protection needs stronger implementation and reform

He discusses state and central legislative powers, general criminal provisions, pandemic-era protection and a call for stronger protection after the Kolkata tragedy. He contrasts perceived Indian weaknesses with claimed overseas protections.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [26:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=1585s)

Context: Legal descriptions and overseas examples are not verified or current guidance; powers, statutes and provisions require a qualified local lawyer.

#### For assault he urges police involvement and institutional support

He recommends a police complaint following assault, solidarity from colleagues, and involving hospital administration and a lawyer when disputes or threatened cases arise. He warns against handling every case using the same self-directed approach.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [29:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=1788s)

Context: This episode does not provide a complete emergency safety plan or case-specific legal advice.

#### Professional associations can sustain demands for staff protection

He describes the value of a unified professional voice and asks associations such as IMA to maintain pressure for protection rather than allowing attention to fade after each incident.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [31:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=1883s)

Context: Advocacy preferences are not proof that a proposed law will pass or prevent violence.

#### Choose relevant legal expertise, communication and affordable terms

He proposes reviewing lawyers who have handled relevant matters, then assessing whether they understand the problem and whether fees fit the client. He challenges dismissing legal action as mere hassle.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [34:32](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2072s)

Context: Reported successful cases, prestige and higher fees do not guarantee suitability or an outcome.

#### Documentation must make the history, decisions and consent traceable

For malpractice risk he repeatedly emphasises documentation and communication. He cites missing histories, incomplete consent forms or signatures, and files that cannot later establish what happened. Electronic records may help, but he still calls for time and team processes.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [40:12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2412s)

Context: Good records support care and legal review; they do not excuse negligent treatment or guarantee immunity.

#### Avoid promising outcomes merely to reassure a patient

He warns that casual assurances that nothing will happen or that a patient will recover can become problematic when outcomes worsen. He urges deliberate communication despite workload pressure.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [41:24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2484s)

Context: Communication should support informed decisions, not become defensive wording that substitutes for good care.

#### He outlines duty, breach, causation and harm

He says medical-negligence work needs specialised legal understanding and explains duty of care, breach, causation and harm. He uses a reasonable-care and emergency injection example to argue for expert evaluation rather than relying on innocence alone.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [42:59](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2579s)

Context: The captioned attribution of the 1957 Bolam decision to the US Supreme Court is incorrect; this is not a statement of current Indian law or a safe-harbour rule for allergy testing.

#### He wants practical legal literacy taught before a crisis

He supports explicit medical-college teaching and assessment on doctors' legal responsibilities, malpractice and prevention. The conversation links reluctance to discuss risk with delayed preparation.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [46:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2766s)

Context: A curricular recommendation, not verification that any named institution meets these standards.

#### He urges indemnity planning and warns about financial exposure

The host asks about malpractice insurance, and Arora urges doctors to prepare for rare but serious financial consequences rather than assuming nothing will go wrong. He describes legal help interpreting policy language.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [47:37](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2857s)

Context: The asserted 80 percent uninsured figure is unsupported. His description of insurance as mandatory should not be read as a verified universal legal requirement.

#### Check defence costs, compensation limits and personal contribution

He recommends obtaining plain written answers about legal fees, filing costs, lawyer-fee limits, compensation coverage and the doctor's own contribution. He cautions against removing cover just to reduce premiums.

Dr Sidharth Arora; host premises and disagreements distinguished; Hindi/Devanagari captions paraphrased in English · [48:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=uOmfdCI-gvc&t=2928s)

Context: Insurer performance and policy adequacy are not verified; wording, exclusions, notification and eligibility require policy-specific review.

#### Patient availability is a concrete clinical-training question

The speakers describe students being required to find patients for final practical examinations when routine clinic flow is insufficient. The guest worries about competition for cases across PG students, interns and undergraduates.

They recount anecdotes about students paying or negotiating with patients to attend examinations and last-minute demands affecting candidates. The guest also recognises that patients may be anxious about a trainee providing care.

Dr. Prathamesh Kshatriya, dentist, implantology practitioner and educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [17:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Anqt97lL0kw&t=1039s)

### Culture, safety & ethics

What support, safeguards and professional boundaries matter?

#### Clear, respectful communication is a learnable clinical skill

He recommends learning to explain problems in understandable language, reducing unnecessary hierarchy and involving the patient in the plan. He values trust and empathy over a distant, godlike role.

Dr. Prathamesh Kshatriya, dentist, implantology practitioner and educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [31:18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Anqt97lL0kw&t=1878s)

Context: Introverts can be excellent clinicians; social style does not determine success. Friendly communication still needs professional boundaries, informed consent and accurate claims.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I explain options, costs, uncertainty and prevention while listening to the patient?

#### Training and legal scope both matter for injectables

She says facial injections need proper training, distinguishes BDS graduates from some postgraduate maxillofacial surgeons and warns that poor technique can harm appearance.

Dr. Himani Joshi, introduced as oral and maxillofacial surgeon/educator; host questions separated; Hindi/English captions contain lost numerical digits and inconsistent rank introductions. · [34:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AaVTwRMYsGk&t=2094s)

Context: Her permission claim is not a legal determination; a short course alone does not establish scope or specialist status.

Question to investigate (editorial): Do current professional rules, registration, competence, privileges and indemnity permit this exact procedure?

#### Fellowships need scrutiny of supervision, recognition and case access

He describes implantology or endodontic fellowships as ways some BDS graduates develop skills and do referral work. He focuses on learning quality rather than simply the duration label.

Dr. Prathamesh Kshatriya, dentist, implantology practitioner and educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [40:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Anqt97lL0kw&t=2435s)

Context: A private fellowship is not automatically equivalent to MDS or a specialist qualification. A BDS graduate cannot infer permission to perform every procedure; competence, registration and privileges must be verified.

Question to investigate (editorial): Is the course recognised for my goal, with supervised cases, assessment and lawful scope?

#### Preventive dental care matters without exaggerated cancer claims

The discussion argues that people often delay visits until pain is severe and that dentists can identify concerning oral lesions and provide preventive advice.

Dr. Prathamesh Kshatriya, dentist, implantology practitioner and educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [50:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Anqt97lL0kw&t=3043s)

Context: The claims that untreated teeth cause thyroid cancer or that a lesion will definitely become cancer are unsupported. Risks differ, symptoms need assessment, and visit frequency should be individualised rather than presented as a universal rule.

Question to investigate (editorial): Does this training emphasise prevention, early assessment and appropriate referral as well as procedures?

#### A root-canal recommendation cannot be judged from a brief complaint

The host asks about unnecessary root canals; she distinguishes possible unethical care, incomplete training and a treatment that may in fact be indicated despite a small-looking surface cavity. She mentions tooth-preserving alternatives and challenges assuming misconduct without facts, then the interview closes.
