#### Public education can begin simply and remain professional

He suggests sharing relevant expertise rather than copying entertainment trends and says a phone can be sufficient to begin. He views online explanations as a way to demonstrate work and build recognition.

Dr. Prathamesh Kshatriya, dentist, implantology practitioner and educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [34:44](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Anqt97lL0kw&t=2084s)

Context: Views and virality do not establish quality. Patient privacy, consent, evidence, professional advertising rules and conflicts matter; social-media work is optional.

Question to investigate (editorial): What useful, accurate information can I share without making patient care a sales catalogue?

#### The discussion links limited public capacity with affordability

He asks why subsidised dental education and public dental services have not expanded alongside private colleges. His concern is access for families who cannot afford high fees or treatment charges.

Dr. Prathamesh Kshatriya, dentist, implantology practitioner and educator; host Dr. Nachiket Bhatia · [12:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Anqt97lL0kw&t=763s)

Context: Institution counts and claims that public care is always free are unverified. More seats alone do not guarantee adequate cases, staffing or jobs.

Question to investigate (editorial): What affordable training and patient-service routes exist locally?

### Shared training and wider residency discussion

These are general preparation or training discussions, not findings about the specialty as a whole.

#### She explains why disease may need treatment before pain develops

She avoids declaring all dentists free of misconduct but says absence of pain can cause patients to misunderstand preventive findings. She supports asking for explanations and a second opinion.

Dr. Himani Joshi, introduced as oral and maxillofacial surgeon/educator; host questions separated; Hindi/English captions contain lost numerical digits and inconsistent rank introductions. · [18:29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AaVTwRMYsGk&t=1109s)

Context: A second opinion need not agree, and trust should not mean following every recommendation without questions.

#### She warns against choosing unregistered treatment only for price

She describes assistants or technicians allegedly opening clinics and reports seeing harm, urging patients to check appropriately qualified care.

Dr. Himani Joshi, introduced as oral and maxillofacial surgeon/educator; host questions separated; Hindi/English captions contain lost numerical digits and inconsistent rank introductions. · [40:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AaVTwRMYsGk&t=2458s)

Context: Specific incidents and cancer causation are unverified; technicians have legitimate roles within their permitted scope, and high price alone does not prove quality.

#### She closes with ambition rather than a concrete exam plan

Asked for a message to MDS aspirants, she encourages thinking ambitiously and not ruling oneself out before trying.

Dr. Himani Joshi, introduced as oral and maxillofacial surgeon/educator; host questions separated; Hindi/English captions contain lost numerical digits and inconsistent rank introductions. · [48:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=AaVTwRMYsGk&t=2934s)

Context: Optimism does not guarantee selection; the host's rank descriptions conflict between the opening and closing.

#### She reports humiliating treatment and withheld learning access

She recounts being removed from the department for speaking to a disfavoured senior, harsh punishment, observed slapping and restrictions on patient contact. She also describes hearing discriminatory comments related to caste, colour, language, appearance and gender.

Dr Himani Joshi; Hindi/Devanagari captions translated and paraphrased in English; host disagreements and unverified allegations distinguished separately · [6:38](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=idBBfFaTMyk&t=398s)

Context: These are personal recollections and reports, not adjudicated findings about current institutions; discrimination is not justified by training.

#### A bleeding-complication example raises institutional responsibility

She describes a serious bleeding event during an extraction associated with a vascular lesion and challenges placing all blame on a new resident without adequate preparation. The point is safe supervision and institutional accountability.

Dr Himani Joshi; Hindi/Devanagari captions translated and paraphrased in English; host disagreements and unverified allegations distinguished separately · [8:05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=idBBfFaTMyk&t=485s)

Context: The account is incomplete and unverified; responsibility for a particular event cannot be assigned from the interview.

#### Non-academic demands and degrading comments are separately criticised

She reports historical demands in another training setting for food and gifts and says this was not the same culture she experienced at Maulana Azad. She gives further examples of degrading comments, clarifying that not all happened personally to her.

Dr Himani Joshi; Hindi/Devanagari captions translated and paraphrased in English; host disagreements and unverified allegations distinguished separately · [9:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=idBBfFaTMyk&t=550s)

Context: Preserve the distinction between first-hand and heard reports; do not attribute every example to the same institution.

#### Her explanation for toxicity is a perception, not a diagnosis

Asked why some seniors normalise harsh treatment, she speculates about frustration, envy of publications and student popularity, while acknowledging different kinds of people exist everywhere and that she does not know the reason.

Dr Himani Joshi; Hindi/Devanagari captions translated and paraphrased in English; host disagreements and unverified allegations distinguished separately · [10:55](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=idBBfFaTMyk&t=655s)

Context: Do not diagnose professors or generalise that government employees are dissatisfied or abusive.

#### Educational videos cannot substitute for demonstrated procedural competence

A debated segment describes learning new procedures from online surgical videos when basic knowledge exists. She sees video clarity as useful and encourages some daring; the host raises concern about unqualified practice.

Dr Himani Joshi; Hindi/Devanagari captions translated and paraphrased in English; host disagreements and unverified allegations distinguished separately · [24:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=idBBfFaTMyk&t=1450s)

Context: Do not interpret confidence or a YouTube video as authorisation to attempt an unfamiliar operation. Videos are supplementary learning, not a substitute for appropriate supervised training, consent and credentialing.

## Shared Career, Training & Wellbeing

13/13 mapped primary episodes have full-caption summaries; 0 have partial selected-caption briefs; 0 related episodes mapped separately.

Personal fit (editorial): Which working environment and personal constraints matter most to me?

### Fit & daily work

Which parts of the actual work would I enjoy?

#### Respect and childhood familiarity initially attracted him to medicine

He recalls frequent childhood visits to a paediatrician, admiration for doctors' status, family encouragement and an interest in biology. He describes medicine versus engineering as the narrow choice he perceived at the time.

Dr Rahul Chawla, neurologist, writer and doctor-rights advocate; host claims distinguished; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [2:19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NRzteRdUA3U&t=139s)

Context: A personal retrospective account. Weak mathematics or family preference is not a general test of medical suitability.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which parts of my preference come from actual work exposure, and which from prestige or a limited picture of available careers?

#### He distinguishes willingness to study from willingness to endure abuse

He says he knew training would be long and academically demanding, but did not anticipate harassment, blame for deaths, intense competition and prolonged sleepless duties. Knowing these conditions might have changed his choice; he would give his children a fuller picture while leaving the decision to them.

Dr Rahul Chawla, neurologist, writer and doctor-rights advocate; host claims distinguished; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [3:04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NRzteRdUA3U&t=184s)

Context: His experience and current preference do not establish that every institution works this way or that no one should study medicine.

Question to investigate (editorial): What do current trainees say about actual duties, support and conduct before I accept this route?

#### After DM he worked while exploring writing, teaching and counselling

He says he finished DM in 2023, continued clinical work and took a more relaxed approach to explore scripts, teaching, social-media posting and helping applicants choose specialties. He hesitated to commit immediately to a private practice while unsure about location and future plans.

Dr Rahul Chawla, neurologist, writer and doctor-rights advocate; host claims distinguished; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [20:16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NRzteRdUA3U&t=1216s)

Context: This was not a statement that he stopped all paid work. His account does not demonstrate that every clinician can access the same time or options.

Question to investigate (editorial): Can I create a financially workable period to explore alternatives without assuming I must immediately build a practice?

#### He wants medicine to occupy part of his life, not all of it

He describes daily regret about aspects of the profession and wants sleep, a defined working day, family and writing time. He says he takes clinical duties seriously and wants to excel, but does not want to give the profession every hour.

Dr Rahul Chawla, neurologist, writer and doctor-rights advocate; host claims distinguished; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [21:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NRzteRdUA3U&t=1286s)

Context: His eight/eight/eight description is an aspiration, not a measured rota or a universal prescription. Serious professional commitment does not require having medicine as one's only identity.

Question to investigate (editorial): What does a satisfying life require outside work, and which real job arrangements can protect those needs?

#### Writing remained a real interest despite rejected scripts

He describes a novel and film scripts, including unsuccessful pitches, and says these interests are part of who he is. He imagines that another profession might have allowed more space for them.

Dr Rahul Chawla, neurologist, writer and doctor-rights advocate; host claims distinguished; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [22:58](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NRzteRdUA3U&t=1378s)

Context: A counterfactual about engineering cannot establish that another career would have been easier or more successful. Rejected work is not proof that exploration had no value.

Question to investigate (editorial): Which ambitions would I regret never testing, and what realistic time and financial boundaries would a trial need?

#### Peer pressure helped carry him into MD while UPSC remained unattempted

He says he prepared for UPSC around final year but never sat the examination. Friends encouraged him to sit a postgraduate entrance despite limited interest; selection into medicine and subsequent work displaced the earlier plan.

Dr Rahul Chawla, neurologist, writer and doctor-rights advocate; host claims distinguished; Hindi captions paraphrased in English · [25:43](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NRzteRdUA3U&t=1543s)

Context: A historical admission story, not current eligibility advice or evidence that an apparently reluctant entrant cannot become a capable doctor.

Question to investigate (editorial): Am I choosing the next course because it fits my goals, or because selection and peer expectations create momentum?

#### A trusted listener helps only when they are ready to listen

She turns open communication into sharing rota constraints and agreeing a realistic time to call. A few free minutes may be needed for food, rest and basic care; missed contact need not automatically mean indifference.

#### Identify triggers and build individual coping skills

She frames personal growth as noticing triggers, recognising how stress is displaced onto others and changing habitual responses. Journaling, breathing, movement, food and sleep are offered as possible tools rather than one universal solution.

#### Anxiety and an anxiety disorder are different

The guest distinguishes ordinary anticipation before an examination or presentation from distress that prevents sleep, eating, concentration or work. A more anxious personality alone does not establish a disorder.

She argues that sleep deserves respect rather than being equated with laziness. Food, exercise and supportive relationships are discussed as everyday contributors to wellbeing.

#### Use small practical tools for overwhelm and procrastination

Writing thoughts down, planning the next day or week, taking a short break and mindful breathing are suggested as options when tasks feel unmanageable. She says it is acceptable to arrive for help without a polished explanation.

If permitted, stepping away briefly, drinking water or pausing to reconnect with the surroundings are suggested as ways to interrupt panic. The guest also discusses slow breathing and returning to questions once clearer.

Context: Specific alleged seat reductions elsewhere are hearsay. More trainees are not the only solution; posts need funding, supervision, appropriate duties and safe limits for all staff.

#### He thinks waiting for juniors can reproduce an unsafe hierarchy

He says problems can be dismissed as something that will disappear once a new junior batch arrives. He worries that repeatedly questioning the system risks being labeled uncooperative, though he says he was not formally labeled a non-worker.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [30:23](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=1823s)

Context: This is his interpretation of the culture and should not become a claim about every resident's motives.

#### A reported meal-break confrontation became a turning point

He recounts missing meals, sleeping very little and stopping for food while returning from assigned tasks. He alleges a senior secretly filmed him and a co-resident, then publicly scolded them for missing rounds, including belittling mental-health needs and other specialties.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [32:25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=1945s)

Context: The account and recording are not independently verified. A short meal break after deprivation is not evidence of laziness, and psychiatry or nonclinical branches should not be used as insults.

#### Unpredictable rounds and missing communication complicated the incident

He says rounds were not at one fixed time and residents normally received a call. He contrasts colleagues who managed the situation without escalating it with the senior who allegedly punished them.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [35:39](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2139s)

Context: Specific colleagues' intentions are his interpretation. Communication failures should be investigated fairly rather than presumed deliberate evasion.

#### He wants advocacy against toxicity to be matched by everyday behavior

He says seeing people involved in earlier mistreatment later participating in a protest felt contradictory. He also acknowledges that many protesters were sincere and some seniors had shielded juniors from unnecessary hostility.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [38:35](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2315s)

Context: This is his perception of unnamed people. It does not prove that a participant's later advocacy is insincere or that no one can change.

#### He says direct clarification could have replaced secret recording and humiliation

He argues that a question about rounds would have allowed an explanation. He alleges the recording was shared as a disappearing message and says he cannot provide it; he also describes the relevant professor as kind.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [39:54](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2394s)

Context: The unavailable recording and messages cannot be independently checked. Avoid attributing the conduct of one reported senior to every supervisor or the whole specialty.

#### The host advocates resident-level information beyond prestige lists

They question using an institution index or brand as a substitute for daily training information. The host promotes his resident-rated initiative as a way to inform later applicants and says a testimony may help someone make a more realistic choice.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [41:36](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2496s)

Context: No index methodology, sample or validation is supplied. Host opinion and this single episode do not justify a definitive institutional safety ranking.

#### They argue for professional responsibility without compulsory personal deference

They criticize the rule that a junior must never miss a senior's call even while doing a hands-on task, and favor clear duties and professional relationships. The host links sustainable hours to staffing.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [44:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2646s)

Context: Broad claims that change is impossible because of age are stereotypes. Responsibility for safe schedules remains institutional rather than resting on a junior's ability to tolerate demands.

#### He reports working while very unwell because asking for leave felt impossible

He says he had recurrent high fever, continued working after symptomatic treatment and felt guilt that absence would burden the few colleagues available. He states that he did not submit a formal leave request and cannot say what would have happened if he had.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [46:14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2774s)

Context: His experience is not proof of a documented refusal. Working with severe illness is not a professional obligation or safe example to follow; this review does not supply treatment or return-to-work advice.

#### He left for home and describes hospital treatment before deciding not to return

He says worsening health led him to leave, seek family support and undergo hospitalization and prolonged treatment. He later remained weak and decided the earlier pattern could not continue. He says the meal incident also changed where he felt safe eating.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [48:45](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=2925s)

Context: The diagnosis and course are self-reported. He explicitly does not claim a direct institutional act caused the illness; the interview cannot establish medical causation. Travel and treatment details are not instructions.

#### He describes supportive personal conversations with the head despite unresolved structural problems

His father delivered a later resignation letter; he says the head offered more recovery time and did not shout or threaten him. He cannot determine the head's overall role in the culture and says their own direct interactions were positive, while staffing issues remained unresolved.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [51:10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=3070s)

Context: Do not collapse this nuanced account into an allegation that the head personally denied leave or caused every event. Knowledge of individual health concerns and administrative responsibility are not established.

#### Prior preparation helped him obtain another result, but his outcome is not guaranteed for others

He says prior conceptual work, revision material and frequent practice tests supported a short focused revision period after leaving. He reports a new rank and hopes for a clinical seat near family.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [52:48](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=3168s)

Context: Ranks, dates and preparation duration are self-reported and internally inconsistent with parts of the introduction. A rapid repeat success is not a reliable promise or an endorsement of a particular paid platform.

#### He emphasizes that a course is not worth sacrificing one's life or health

He says leaving was an option he could ultimately take, including accepting uncertainty or a medical-officer job rather than returning. He and the host stress that life extends beyond one institute or degree.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [54:06](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=3246s)

Context: Resignation is one possible route, not the sole answer to distress or a guarantee of recovery. Urgent danger requires immediate human support and local emergency or mental-health services; no need to wait for an exam or administrative outcome.

#### A closing request for a toxicity ranking goes beyond the evidence he directly observed

The host presses for a department ordering. The guest initially declines to rank beyond his own orthopaedic experience, then discusses medicine, surgery, ENT and anesthesia largely through workload and peer reports.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [55:08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=3308s)

Context: This is not a validated comparative ranking. Secondhand accounts, different types of pressure and posting variation cannot be reduced to one precise order; no current university-wide conclusion is established.

#### The closing urges an informed choice while remaining overly certain about the next placement

The host thanks him for sharing and urges applicants to investigate training conditions and avoid treating one course as the whole of life. He predicts a positive next placement while the guest expresses hope.

Dr Anubhav, a former orthopaedics resident, with host Dr Nachiket Bhatia · [56:26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zD7eFIEHmb8&t=3386s)

Context: A better rank or different brand cannot guarantee a supportive placement. Use multiple current sources, actual terms and a practical support plan.
